# Rivier UI

> A component library for AI-native development: React components you copy into a project and own, themed
> from one place (light or dark, square to round, any highlight colour), covering controls, layout and bento
> grids, motion and transitions, 3D and charts, dates, flows, conversation, media. Built on Radix, Tailwind CSS,
> Motion and three.js. Keyboard operable, right-to-left safe, no fixed words: labels are props.

Install an item into a project: `rivier-ui add <name>` (it brings what the item depends on, and the theme).
Imports in a project: `@/components/<category>/<name>` and `@/lib/cn`.
Rules for using and writing components: CONVENTIONS.md. Theming: registry/theme/rivier-ui.css.

## Helpers

### announce

Says a message to screen-reader users through one shared live region, politely or at once, without moving focus.

Use it: Something changed that a sighted person can see but no focus change will read out: an item was moved, a filter applied, a total changed, a reply finished. Not for content the person is about to read anyway, and not for errors on a field (use the field's own message). A component that is already a live region (status-line, toaster) does not need it.

```tsx
announce("Lunch moved to position 2 of 5");
announce("The connection was lost", "assertive");
```

### cn

Joins class names and resolves Tailwind conflicts, so a class passed in wins over a component's own.

Use it: Every component uses it. Use it wherever classes are combined conditionally.

```tsx
cn("px-4 py-2", isActive && "bg-primary", className)
```

### direction

Tells whether an element reads right to left, and turns "start" and "end" arrow keys and offsets the right way round for it.

Use it: A component handles Left and Right arrow keys, or moves something sideways with a transform, and must work in right-to-left pages. Layout itself needs no code: use logical utilities (ps-, ms-, start-, text-start). To set a direction for part of a page use direction-provider.

```tsx
function onKeyDown(event: KeyboardEvent<HTMLDivElement>) {
  const step = inlineStep(event.key, event.currentTarget); // +1 towards the end, -1 towards the start, 0 otherwise
  if (step !== 0) move(step);
}
```

### explainer-spec

The plain-data description of an explainer film (scenes of a title, a chart, a map, a 3D model, a then-and-now comparison, a quote or a caption, each with a length, a transition, captions, a narration cue and a provenance label) and a validator that lists every fault in words.

Use it: An assistant or a project writes a film as JSON and hands it to motion/explainer. Run validateExplainer first and show its faults: each says where the fault is and how to mend it. For a film drawn by hand from React, use film-stage directly.

```tsx
const spec: ExplainerSpec = {
  title: "How the river rose",
  lang: "en",
  scenes: [
    { id: "intro", kind: "title", duration: 4, title: "How the river rose", subtitle: "Spring 2026" },
    {
      id: "levels", kind: "chart", duration: 8, chart: "line-chart",
      props: { label: "Water level by day", data: [{ day: 1, level: 2.1 }, { day: 2, level: 2.9 }], x: "day", series: [{ key: "level", label: "Level (m)" }] },
      captions: [{ start: 0.5, end: 4, text: "The level rose for four days." }],
      provenance: { kind: "measured", note: "Gauge readings" },
    },
  ],
};
const faults = validateExplainer(spec); // [] when it is sound
```

### motion

The motion tokens as numbers for the motion package (easing, durations, a pointer spring), the useMotionSafe gate, and the entrance engine the reveal components share.

Use it: Any component animated with the motion package: take timing from here so it matches the CSS tokens, and gate on useMotionSafe so server markup is the final state. For CSS transitions use the duration-* and ease-out utilities instead.

```tsx
const safe = useMotionSafe();
return (
  <motion.div
    initial={safe ? { opacity: 0 } : false}
    animate={{ opacity: 1 }}
    transition={{ duration: DURATION.slow, ease: EASE }}
  />
);
```

### theme-color

Resolves a theme CSS variable such as "--highlight" to an rgb() string that three.js and canvas code can parse, and re-reads it when the theme changes.

Use it: Anything that cannot use a Tailwind class or `var()`: three.js materials, canvas drawing. In markup use the token classes (`bg-primary`, `fill-chart-1`) instead.

```tsx
const { "--highlight": highlight, "--foreground": ink } = useThemeColors(["--highlight", "--foreground"]);
material.color.set(highlight);

// Outside React:
const border = readThemeColor("--border");
```

### use-controllable-state

State that a parent may control: it follows `value` when one is given and keeps its own from `defaultValue` when not, calling `onChange` either way.

Use it: Writing a component that should work both controlled (`value` + `onValueChange`) and uncontrolled (`defaultValue`), which every input-like component in the library does. Radix primitives already do this for their own state; use this for state the library adds on top.

```tsx
function Stepper({ value, defaultValue = 0, onValueChange }: { value?: number; defaultValue?: number; onValueChange?: (value: number) => void }) {
  const [count, setCount] = useControllableState({ value, defaultValue, onChange: onValueChange });
  return <button onClick={() => setCount(count + 1)}>{count}</button>;
}
```

### use-media

Follows an audio or video element (playing, time, duration, buffered, volume, rate, text tracks, waiting, error) as React state, with the actions to drive it, the context player parts share, and time formatting through Intl.

Use it: Building player parts around a `<video>` or `<audio>` element the project renders. video-player, audio-player, captions and scene-strip are built on it; use it directly for a control they do not have. The element stays the source of truth: sources, HLS and DRM are attached to it by the project, and nothing here loads or decodes media.

```tsx
function Elapsed() {
  const { state, locale } = useMediaContext("Elapsed");
  return <span>{formatMediaTime(state.time, locale)}</span>;
}

// Without a player around it
const [audio, setAudio] = useState<HTMLAudioElement | null>(null);
const state = useMediaState(audio);
<audio ref={setAudio} src="/note.mp3" />
<Button onClick={() => mediaActions(audio).toggle()}>{state.playing ? "Pause" : "Play"}</Button>
```

### use-size

Measures an element with ResizeObserver and returns its content width and height in whole pixels.

Use it: Drawing to the size of a container: charts, canvases. For layout that only needs to adapt, use container queries (`@container`, `@md:`) instead.

```tsx
const { ref, width, height } = useSize<HTMLDivElement>();
return <div ref={ref} className="aspect-video w-full">{width > 0 && <svg width={width} height={height} />}</div>;
```

## Controls and surfaces

### accordion

Stacked sections whose content opens and closes under its heading.

Use it: Questions and answers, or long settings where people need a few sections out of many. `type="single"` keeps one open (add `collapsible` so it can be closed again); `type="multiple"` lets several be open. For views that replace each other in one place use tabs. Do not hide content everyone needs.

```tsx
<Accordion type="single" collapsible defaultValue="shipping">
  <AccordionItem value="shipping">
    <AccordionTrigger>How long does delivery take?</AccordionTrigger>
    <AccordionContent>Two to four working days.</AccordionContent>
  </AccordionItem>
  <AccordionItem value="returns">
    <AccordionTrigger>Can I send it back?</AccordionTrigger>
    <AccordionContent>Yes, within thirty days.</AccordionContent>
  </AccordionItem>
</Accordion>
```

### alert

A message in the page with an icon, a title, a description and an optional action. Four variants: info, success, warning, destructive.

Use it: Telling the reader something about the page or the result of an action, in place. For a message that appears and leaves use a toast; for one that needs an answer use a dialog.

```tsx
<Alert variant="success">
  <AlertTitle>Payment received</AlertTitle>
  <AlertDescription>A receipt is on its way to your inbox.</AlertDescription>
</Alert>
<Alert variant="destructive">
  <AlertTitle>The card was declined</AlertTitle>
  <AlertDescription>Check the number and the expiry date, then try again.</AlertDescription>
  <AlertAction><Button size="sm" variant="outline">Try again</Button></AlertAction>
</Alert>
```

### audio-player

The parts of a sound player around an `<audio>` element: play, a waveform that is also the time bar, time, speed and mute.

Use it: A voice note, a recording, a clip of music or narration a person plays and seeks in. The project gives the element its source and, for the waveform, the peaks (computed ahead of time, or with computePeaks for a short clip); without peaks the bar is a flat line of the same size. Offer a Transcript (from captions) for anything spoken. Nothing plays by itself. For video use video-player; for a plain time bar without a waveform use scrubber.

```tsx
<AudioPlayer aria-label="Voice note from Ana">
  <AudioPlayerAudio src="/note.mp3" />
  <AudioPlayerPlay />
  <AudioPlayerWaveform peaks={peaks} />
  <AudioPlayerTime />
  <AudioPlayerRate />
  <AudioPlayerMute />
</AudioPlayer>

// Peaks for a short clip, in the browser
const peaks = await computePeaks(await (await fetch("/note.mp3")).arrayBuffer(), 64);
```

### avatar

A round picture of a person or a team, with initials shown until the image loads or when it fails, and a group that overlaps.

Use it: Showing who something belongs to. Always give AvatarFallback initials; give AvatarImage an alt (the name), or alt="" when the name is printed next to it.

```tsx
<Avatar size="lg">
  <AvatarImage src="/people/hana.jpg" alt="Hana Ito" />
  <AvatarFallback>HI</AvatarFallback>
</Avatar>
<AvatarGroup aria-label="Team">
  <Avatar><AvatarFallback>AK</AvatarFallback></Avatar>
  <Avatar><AvatarFallback>BL</AvatarFallback></Avatar>
  <Avatar><AvatarFallback>+3</AvatarFallback></Avatar>
</AvatarGroup>
```

### badge

A small label for a status, a count or a category. Six variants and an optional leading dot.

Use it: Marking a state or a tag next to other content. It is not clickable: for a removable or selectable chip use a button with size "sm".

```tsx
<Badge>New</Badge>
<Badge variant="soft">Beta</Badge>
<Badge variant="success" dot>Live</Badge>
<Badge variant="outline">Draft</Badge>
```

### bottom-sheet

A panel that rises from the bottom edge, rests at one of several heights (snap points), and can be dragged between them or down to dismiss, with a keyboard handle that does the same.

Use it: Phones first: details, filters, a picker or a secondary task that should stay within reach of the thumb and may be peeked at before it is opened fully. With `modal={false}` it stays open while the page behind is used (a player, a route summary). For a panel from a side edge, or one with no snap points on a desktop, use sheet; for a short decision use dialog; beside the content on wide screens use dock. Always give it a BottomSheetTitle (add className="sr-only" to hide it). Opened by state with no BottomSheetTrigger, focus does not return on close: refocus the opener in `onCloseAutoFocus` on BottomSheetContent.

```tsx
<BottomSheet snapPoints={[0.4, 0.9]}>
  <BottomSheetTrigger asChild><Button variant="outline">Details</Button></BottomSheetTrigger>
  <BottomSheetContent>
    <BottomSheetHandle />
    <BottomSheetHeader>
      <BottomSheetTitle>Saturday</BottomSheetTitle>
      <BottomSheetDescription>Three things planned.</BottomSheetDescription>
    </BottomSheetHeader>
    <BottomSheetBody>…</BottomSheetBody>
    <BottomSheetFooter>
      <BottomSheetClose asChild><Button>Done</Button></BottomSheetClose>
    </BottomSheetFooter>
  </BottomSheetContent>
</BottomSheet>

// Controlled, in pixels and rems, staying open while the page is used
<BottomSheet open={open} onOpenChange={setOpen} snapPoints={["6rem", "320px", 1]} snap={snap} onSnapChange={setSnap} modal={false} dismissible={false}>
  …
</BottomSheet>
```

### breadcrumb

The path from the top of the site to the current page, as links with separators.

Use it: Pages nested three or more levels deep, above the page title. The last item is the current page: a BreadcrumbPage, not a link. For moving between sibling pages use tabs or the navbar. With a router link, pass it through `asChild`.

```tsx
<Breadcrumb>
  <BreadcrumbList>
    <BreadcrumbItem><BreadcrumbLink href="/">Home</BreadcrumbLink></BreadcrumbItem>
    <BreadcrumbSeparator />
    <BreadcrumbItem><BreadcrumbLink href="/projects">Projects</BreadcrumbLink></BreadcrumbItem>
    <BreadcrumbSeparator />
    <BreadcrumbItem><BreadcrumbPage>Atlas</BreadcrumbPage></BreadcrumbItem>
  </BreadcrumbList>
</Breadcrumb>
```

### button

A button, or a link that looks like one. Five variants, three sizes, a loading state.

Use it: Any action. One "solid" per view for the main action; "outline" or "ghost" for the rest; "destructive" only for deleting.

```tsx
<Button>Save</Button>
<Button variant="outline" size="sm">Cancel</Button>
<Button asChild><a href="/pricing">See pricing</a></Button>
<Button loading>Saving</Button>
```

### calendar

A month grid for choosing a day, several days or a range of days, with days that can be unavailable for a stated reason and days that carry a mark. Days are plain "YYYY-MM-DD" strings, so no time zone can move them.

Use it: Choosing dates where seeing the month matters: a booking, a stay, a deadline. It stays on the page; to open it from a field use date-picker. Never use the browser's native date input beside it. For a date far in the past that the person knows by heart (a birthday) three plain fields are quicker. Pass `locale` (the page's language) so that names, numerals and the first day of the week are right; without it the calendar is in English.

```tsx
// One day (uncontrolled), with days that cannot be chosen and days that carry a word
<Calendar
  locale="en-GB"
  defaultValue="2026-11-14"
  min="2026-11-01"
  disabled={(day) => (closed.has(day) ? "nothing open" : false)}
  marks={(day) => (busy.has(day) ? "busy" : undefined)}
/>

// A range (controlled), two months where there is room
const [stay, setStay] = useState<CalendarRange>({ start: null, end: null });
<Calendar mode="range" value={stay} onValueChange={setStay} numberOfMonths={2} locale="en-GB" />

// Several days, and its own layout with a footer
<Calendar mode="multiple" defaultValue={["2026-11-03", "2026-11-05"]}>
  <CalendarPrevious />
  <CalendarNext />
  <CalendarMonths />
  <p className="px-1 pt-2 text-sm text-muted-foreground">A dot marks a busy day.</p>
</Calendar>
```

### captions

Captions drawn by the page instead of the browser, on a solid ground that reads on any picture, and a transcript: every line of a clip as a list that can be pressed to go there.

Use it: Inside video-player (Captions sits above the controls and moves with them) or beside audio-player (Transcript, or Captions with `inline`). Captions are for people who cannot hear the sound; a Transcript is also the alternative for people who cannot see or play it, so offer one for anything spoken. The lines come from a caption track of the media element (`<track kind="captions">`), or from `cues` the project passes. Not a live region: with the sound on, a screen reader would talk over it.

```tsx
// In a video player: the lines of the element's caption track
<VideoPlayer aria-label="Loading the kiln" defaultCaptions>
  <VideoPlayerVideo src="/kiln.mp4"><track kind="captions" src="/kiln.en.vtt" srcLang="en" label="English" /></VideoPlayerVideo>
  <Captions />
  <VideoPlayerControls>…</VideoPlayerControls>
</VideoPlayer>

// Beside an audio player: cues from the project, as a transcript
const cues = [{ start: 0, end: 4, text: "Welcome." }, { start: 4, end: 9, text: "This is the yard." }];
<AudioPlayer aria-label="A walk through the yard">
  <AudioPlayerAudio src="/yard.mp3" />
  <AudioPlayerPlay /> <AudioPlayerWaveform peaks={peaks} />
  <Transcript cues={cues} aria-label="Transcript" lang="en" />
</AudioPlayer>
```

### card

A flat surface with a hairline edge, and parts for a header, title, description, content and footer.

Use it: Grouping related content: a plan, a stat, a form section. For a grid of unequal cards use bento-grid.

```tsx
<Card>
  <CardHeader>
    <CardTitle>Usage</CardTitle>
    <CardDescription>This month</CardDescription>
  </CardHeader>
  <CardContent>1,204 requests</CardContent>
  <CardFooter><Button size="sm">Details</Button></CardFooter>
</Card>
```

### carousel

A row of slides that is scrolled sideways one at a time (or a few at a time), with previous and next buttons, dots or a count, keys, and an optional autoplay that always has a pause button.

Use it: A handful of pictures or cards of equal weight where one (or a few) is enough at a time: the photos of a place, featured items, quotes. It is the browser's own scrolling with CSS scroll snap, so a swipe, a trackpad and momentum work as they do everywhere, right-to-left pages mirror by themselves and nothing moves under reduced motion; no carousel package is used (Embla, MIT, moves slides with transforms on its own engine, which this does not need). Set how many slides show with a basis on the slides (`className="basis-1/2 md:basis-1/3"`). Do not hide content a person must read in a carousel, and do not autoplay anything with text to read. For looking at pictures large use gallery with lightbox; for scenes of a clip use scene-strip; for thousands of items use virtual-list.

```tsx
<Carousel aria-label="Rooms">
  <CarouselViewport>
    {rooms.map((room) => (
      <CarouselSlide key={room.id}>
        <img src={room.picture} alt={room.name} className="aspect-video w-full object-cover" />
      </CarouselSlide>
    ))}
  </CarouselViewport>
  <div className="flex items-center justify-between gap-2">
    <CarouselPrevious />
    <CarouselDots />
    <CarouselNext />
  </div>
</Carousel>

// Controlled, three to a view on wide screens, with a count; and one that plays by itself
<Carousel index={index} onIndexChange={setIndex} aria-label="Featured">
  <CarouselViewport>{cards.map((card) => <CarouselSlide key={card.id} className="basis-full md:basis-1/3">…</CarouselSlide>)}</CarouselViewport>
  <CarouselPrevious /> <CarouselCount /> <CarouselNext />
</Carousel>
<Carousel autoplay={5000} loop aria-label="Highlights">
  <CarouselViewport>…</CarouselViewport>
  <CarouselPlayPause /> <CarouselPrevious /> <CarouselNext />
</Carousel>
```

### certainty-legend

A small key of three or four named classes (how sure something is, or any other kind), each with its own pattern as well as its own colour, where each class can be switched off and on.

Use it: A scene, a map, a drawing or a chart marks its parts by class and the reader needs the key and a way to hide a class: what is recorded, what is worked out, what is a guess. The project supplies the names; the legend reports which classes are shown (`onValueChange`) and the project applies that to its own scene. Use CertaintySwatch to draw the same pattern in the scene's own key or in a caption. The pattern is what tells classes apart for someone who cannot tell the colours apart, so use it in the scene too. For filters with no key use chip; for the series of a chart, the chart's own legend.

```tsx
const classes = [
  { id: "recorded", label: "Recorded", description: "Measured on site" },
  { id: "inferred", label: "Inferred", description: "Worked out from what remains" },
  { id: "imagined", label: "Imagined", description: "A guess, drawn to complete the picture" },
];
<CertaintyLegend aria-label="How sure each part is" classes={classes} defaultValue={["recorded", "inferred", "imagined"]} onValueChange={(shown) => scene.show(shown)} />

// The same pattern elsewhere
<CertaintySwatch pattern="hatch" tone={2} />
```

### checkbox

A checkbox with checked, unchecked and indeterminate states.

Use it: Choosing any number of options, or agreeing to something that is submitted with a form. For a setting that applies at once use switch; for exactly one of several use radio-group.

```tsx
<Label><Checkbox defaultChecked /> Email me product news</Label>
<Checkbox checked="indeterminate" aria-label="Select all rows" />
```

### chip

A small pill for one short value: a filter that is on and can be removed, a suggestion to press, or one of a set of choices that can be switched on and off.

Use it: Filters in effect above a list (Chip with ChipRemove), suggested replies or refinements under a message or a search (ChipButton), and choosing one or several short options such as moods, tags or times of day (ChipGroup). For a status that cannot be pressed use badge; for two to five views of the same thing use segmented-control; for long labels use checkboxes or radio-group.

```tsx
// Filters in effect
<Chip>Under 50 <ChipRemove aria-label="Remove the filter: under 50" onClick={clearPrice} /></Chip>

// Suggestions
<ChipButton onClick={() => ask("Only this weekend")}>Only this weekend</ChipButton>

// A set of choices: several can be on (type="multiple") or one (type="single")
<ChipGroup type="multiple" defaultValue={["calm"]} aria-label="Mood">
  <ChipGroupItem value="calm">Calm</ChipGroupItem>
  <ChipGroupItem value="lively">Lively</ChipGroupItem>
</ChipGroup>
```

### combobox

A select with a search field: a button that shows the choice and opens a list that narrows as one types.

Use it: Choosing one value from a list too long to scan: a country, a city, a person, a product. Under about eight options use select (or radio-group, or segmented-control for two to five); for running actions rather than choosing a value use command; for several values use chip or checkboxes. Name the trigger with a Label (`htmlFor` its `id`) or `aria-label`. Each item's `value` is what is stored; what is typed is matched against the item's text.

```tsx
const CITIES = [{ value: "lis", label: "Lisbon" }, { value: "opo", label: "Porto" }];
const [city, setCity] = useState("");

<Combobox value={city} onValueChange={setCity} name="city">
  <ComboboxTrigger aria-label="City" className="w-56">
    <ComboboxValue placeholder="Choose a city">{CITIES.find((item) => item.value === city)?.label}</ComboboxValue>
  </ComboboxTrigger>
  <ComboboxContent aria-label="Cities">
    <ComboboxInput placeholder="Search cities" />
    <ComboboxList>
      <ComboboxEmpty>No city found.</ComboboxEmpty>
      {CITIES.map((item) => (
        <ComboboxItem key={item.value} value={item.value}>{item.label}</ComboboxItem>
      ))}
    </ComboboxList>
  </ComboboxContent>
</Combobox>
```

### command

A command palette: a search field over a filtered, keyboard-driven list of actions, inline or in a dialog.

Use it: Fast access to many actions or pages by typing (the Ctrl/Cmd+K palette), or a searchable list inside a popover. For a handful of actions use dropdown-menu. CommandDialog is usually opened by a shortcut, with no trigger, so focus has nowhere to return: remember the opener (`opener.current = document.activeElement` before opening) and refocus it in `onCloseAutoFocus={(event) => { event.preventDefault(); opener.current?.focus(); }}`.

```tsx
const [open, setOpen] = useState(false);

<Button variant="outline" onClick={() => setOpen(true)}>Search</Button>
<CommandDialog open={open} onOpenChange={setOpen}>
  <CommandInput placeholder="Type a command" />
  <CommandList>
    <CommandEmpty>Nothing found.</CommandEmpty>
    <CommandGroup heading="Pages">
      <CommandItem onSelect={() => setOpen(false)}>Dashboard</CommandItem>
      <CommandItem onSelect={() => setOpen(false)}>Settings <CommandShortcut>Ctrl ,</CommandShortcut></CommandItem>
    </CommandGroup>
    <CommandSeparator />
    <CommandGroup heading="Account">
      <CommandItem onSelect={() => setOpen(false)}>Sign out</CommandItem>
    </CommandGroup>
  </CommandList>
</CommandDialog>
```

### compare-slider

Two layers of the same size, one over the other, with a divider that is dragged or moved with the keyboard to show more of one and less of the other: then and now, before and after.

Use it: Comparing two views of the same thing in the same frame: two pictures, two maps, two 3D viewers, any two children. Each side has a visible name. The divider is a slider, so it works without dragging. The frame is drawn left to right in every language (a picture is not mirrored in a right-to-left page), so the first layer is always on the left and the arrow keys move the divider the way they point. For two things that are not the same view use two cards side by side; for many pictures use gallery or carousel.

```tsx
<CompareSlider aspect={16 / 9} labels={{ first: "1930", second: "Today" }} aria-label="The square in 1930 and today">
  <CompareSliderFirst><img src="/square-1930.jpg" alt="The square in 1930: a tram stop and a kiosk" /></CompareSliderFirst>
  <CompareSliderSecond><img src="/square-today.jpg" alt="The square today: trees and a fountain" /></CompareSliderSecond>
  <CompareSliderLabels />
  <CompareSliderHandle />
</CompareSlider>

// Controlled, with any two children
<CompareSlider value={split} onValueChange={setSplit} labels={{ first: "Survey", second: "Reconstruction" }} aria-label="Survey and reconstruction">
  <CompareSliderFirst><SurveyView /></CompareSliderFirst>
  <CompareSliderSecond><ReconstructionView /></CompareSliderSecond>
  <CompareSliderLabels />
  <CompareSliderHandle />
</CompareSlider>
```

### compare-table

Two to four things side by side, attribute by attribute: a table whose first column (the attribute names) stays in view while the things scroll sideways inside it on narrow screens.

Use it: Helping someone choose between a few similar things: plans, products, places, quotes. Give every thing the same rows, in the same order. For plain rows of data use table; for more than four things let people pick which to compare first; for one thing's details use a description list or card.

```tsx
<CompareTable label="Compare the two plans" columns={2} onlyDifferences={onlyDifferences}>
  <CompareHeader corner="Plan">
    <CompareColumn><CompareColumnTitle>Starter</CompareColumnTitle><Button size="sm">Choose</Button></CompareColumn>
    <CompareColumn><CompareColumnTitle>Team</CompareColumnTitle><Button size="sm">Choose</Button></CompareColumn>
  </CompareHeader>
  <CompareGroup title="Basics">
    <CompareRow label="Price a month">
      <CompareCell value={12} best>€12</CompareCell>
      <CompareCell value={29}>€29</CompareCell>
    </CompareRow>
    <CompareRow label="Support">
      <CompareCell value="email">By email</CompareCell>
      <CompareCell value="email">By email</CompareCell>
    </CompareRow>
  </CompareGroup>
</CompareTable>
```

### composer

The box a person writes a message in: a field that grows with the text, a list of attachments, and a toolbar with slots for an attach button, a voice button and send (which becomes stop while a reply is on its way).

Use it: Under a thread, or anywhere a person sends free text to an assistant or to other people. It owns the text and the keys (Enter sends, Shift+Enter makes a new line, nothing is sent while an input method is composing); the project owns the files, the microphone and the sending. For one line with no attachments (a search box) use input-group; for a long form field use textarea.

```tsx
<Composer onSubmit={send} busy={replying} onStop={stop}>
  <ComposerAttachments aria-label="Attachments">
    {files.map((file) => (
      <ComposerAttachment key={file.name} onRemove={() => remove(file)} removeLabel={`Remove ${file.name}`}>{file.name}</ComposerAttachment>
    ))}
  </ComposerAttachments>
  <ComposerInput aria-label="Message" placeholder="Ask anything" />
  <ComposerToolbar>
    <ComposerAttachButton aria-label="Attach a file" onFiles={add} accept="image/*" multiple />
    <ComposerVoiceButton pressed={listening} onPressedChange={setListening} />
    <ComposerSubmit />
  </ComposerToolbar>
</Composer>
```

### consent

Asks permission before something is switched on or shared: what is asked for, item by item, each optional one with its own switch that starts off, and two equal buttons to allow or decline. As a sheet (ConsentSheet) or in the page (ConsentPanel).

Use it: Before sharing a person's data with another party, connecting an account, turning on an assistant or a feature that reads their content, or using a device permission. One consent per purpose, in plain words, at the moment it is needed. Nothing is pre-ticked and declining is as easy as allowing. For a yes or no about an action the person just started (delete, leave) use dialog; for a cookie notice use the same parts in a ConsentPanel.

```tsx
<ConsentSheet side="bottom" defaultValue={[]} onAccept={(granted) => connect(granted)} onDecline={skip} onDismiss={skip}>
  <ConsentTrigger asChild><Button>Connect calendar</Button></ConsentTrigger>
  <ConsentContent>
    <ConsentHeader>
      <ConsentTitle>Let the planner see your calendar?</ConsentTitle>
      <ConsentDescription>It is used to avoid times when you are busy. You can stop this in Settings at any time.</ConsentDescription>
    </ConsentHeader>
    <ConsentScopes>
      <ConsentScope value="busy" title="Busy times" description="When you are busy, without what the events are." required requiredLabel="Always needed" />
      <ConsentScope value="titles" title="Event names" description="So that suggestions can mention what you have planned." />
    </ConsentScopes>
    <ConsentDetails summary="How this is stored">Kept for 30 days, never sold, deleted when you disconnect.</ConsentDetails>
    <ConsentFooter>
      <ConsentDecline>Do not allow</ConsentDecline>
      <ConsentAccept>Allow</ConsentAccept>
    </ConsentFooter>
  </ConsentContent>
</ConsentSheet>
```

### context-menu

A menu of actions that opens at the pointer on right-click, and on a long press on touch screens: items, checkbox and radio items, labels, separators, sub-menus and a shortcut slot.

Use it: Shortcuts to actions on a thing in a dense interface (a file, a row, a canvas object). Nothing shows that it exists, so every action in it must also be reachable another way; for a visible button use dropdown-menu.

```tsx
<ContextMenu>
  <ContextMenuTrigger className="flex h-32 items-center justify-center rounded-surface border border-dashed text-sm">
    Right-click, or press and hold
  </ContextMenuTrigger>
  <ContextMenuContent>
    <ContextMenuItem>Open <ContextMenuShortcut>Enter</ContextMenuShortcut></ContextMenuItem>
    <ContextMenuCheckboxItem checked>Pinned</ContextMenuCheckboxItem>
    <ContextMenuSub>
      <ContextMenuSubTrigger>Label</ContextMenuSubTrigger>
      <ContextMenuSubContent>
        <ContextMenuRadioGroup value="none">
          <ContextMenuRadioItem value="none">None</ContextMenuRadioItem>
          <ContextMenuRadioItem value="urgent">Urgent</ContextMenuRadioItem>
        </ContextMenuRadioGroup>
      </ContextMenuSubContent>
    </ContextMenuSub>
    <ContextMenuSeparator />
    <ContextMenuItem variant="destructive">Delete</ContextMenuItem>
  </ContextMenuContent>
</ContextMenu>
```

### countdown

The time left until a moment, as text that counts down ("4 min 12 s"), announced to screen-reader users only at the moments the project lists.

Use it: Something the person holds for a limited time: a reserved seat, a price that is kept, a code that expires, a session about to end. Say what happens at the end and offer a way to get more time beside it. Not for decoration or pressure: a countdown that restarts or means nothing is a dark pattern. For progress through a known amount of work use progress.

```tsx
<p>
  Your seats are held for{" "}
  <Countdown
    to={hold.expiresAt}
    locale="en"
    thresholds={[300, 60]}
    announceAt={(_, left) => `${left} left to finish booking`}
    onExpire={release}
    expiredLabel="no longer: the hold has ended"
  />
</p>
```

### data-grid

A table of records a person works in: sorting by one or several columns, a filter per column and a search across all, grouping with totals, columns pinned to the start, shown and hidden, rows chosen by checkbox, pages or a window of rows for thousands, and cells edited in place; one tab stop and arrow keys from cell to cell, to the WAI-ARIA grid pattern.

Use it: Lists of records that are sorted, narrowed, compared and changed: orders, accounts, files, results. For a few rows to read use table; for side-by-side comparison of two to four things use compare-table; for an endless feed use virtual-list.

```tsx
<DataGrid
  label="Orders"
  rows={orders}
  rowId={(order) => order.id}
  columns={[
    { key: "id", header: "Order", pin: "start", width: 110 },
    { key: "customer", header: "Customer" },
    { key: "status", header: "Status" },
    { key: "total", header: "Total", type: "number", aggregate: "sum", editable: true },
  ]}
  selectable
  pageSize={20}
  onCellEdit={(id, key, value) => save(id, key, value)}
/>
```

### date-picker

A button that shows a date, or a range of dates, and opens a calendar in a popover to choose it. Values are "YYYY-MM-DD" strings.

Use it: A date or a stay inside a form or a toolbar, where a calendar that is always open would take too much room. When the calendar is the main thing on the screen use calendar itself. Never the browser's native date input. Name the button by passing `aria-labelledby` with the id of its visible label: the chosen date is added to the name.

```tsx
// One day, uncontrolled, submitted with a form as "date"
<p id="date-label">Date</p>
<DatePicker defaultValue="2026-11-14" name="date" locale="en-GB">
  <DatePickerTrigger aria-labelledby="date-label" placeholder="Choose a date" />
  <DatePickerCalendar min="2026-11-01" disabled={(day) => (closed.has(day) ? "nothing open" : false)} />
</DatePicker>

// A range, controlled, two months where there is room
const [stay, setStay] = useState<CalendarRange>({ start: null, end: null });
<DateRangePicker value={stay} onValueChange={setStay} startName="from" endName="to" locale="en-GB">
  <DatePickerTrigger aria-label="Stay" placeholder="Arrival – departure" />
  <DatePickerCalendar numberOfMonths={2} />
</DateRangePicker>
```

### dialog

A modal window over a dimmed page, with parts for a header, title, description and footer.

Use it: A short task or a decision that must be finished or dismissed before going on. For a panel from an edge (menus, filters, details) use sheet; for something small attached to a control use popover. Always give it a DialogTitle (add className="sr-only" to hide it). Opened by a DialogTrigger, focus returns to that trigger on close. Opened by state with no trigger (a shortcut, a menu item), Radix has nothing to return to: remember the opener (`opener.current = document.activeElement` before opening) and refocus it in `onCloseAutoFocus={(event) => { event.preventDefault(); opener.current?.focus(); }}` on DialogContent.

```tsx
<Dialog>
  <DialogTrigger asChild><Button variant="outline">Rename</Button></DialogTrigger>
  <DialogContent>
    <DialogHeader>
      <DialogTitle>Rename project</DialogTitle>
      <DialogDescription>The address of the project does not change.</DialogDescription>
    </DialogHeader>
    <input aria-label="Name" defaultValue="Atlas" className="h-control rounded-control border border-input px-3 text-base" />
    <DialogFooter>
      <DialogClose asChild><Button variant="outline">Cancel</Button></DialogClose>
      <Button>Save</Button>
    </DialogFooter>
  </DialogContent>
</Dialog>
```

### direction-provider

Sets the reading direction (left to right, or right to left) for everything inside it: the `dir` attribute for layout and text, and the context Radix-based components read for arrow keys and placement.

Use it: Once around the app, with the direction of the current language, in any product that has or may get a right-to-left language (Arabic, Hebrew, Persian, Urdu, Dhivehi). Also around one part of a page in the other direction. A product in one left-to-right language does not need it. Put `dir` on <html> as well (the provider's own element covers only what is inside it; menus and dialogs are portalled to <body>). For people's own words in an unknown language use `dir="auto"` on that element instead.

```tsx
// app/layout.tsx
const dir = directionOf(locale); // "rtl" for "ar", "he", "fa", "ur", "dv" …
<html lang={locale} dir={dir}>
  <body>
    <DirectionProvider dir={dir}>{children}</DirectionProvider>
  </body>
</html>

// anywhere below
const dir = useDirection();
```

### dock

A layout of main content with a panel docked beside it that stays while the person works: the panel can be resized with a splitter, collapsed to a slim bar, and on narrow containers gives way to a bar at the bottom.

Use it: A working surface that belongs beside the content and is not modal: a plan next to a conversation, an inspector next to a canvas, details next to a list. For a panel that covers the page for a moment use sheet; for two fixed columns with no resizing use split. Write the parts in reading order: DockMain, DockResizer, DockPanel for a panel at the end; DockPanel, DockResizer, DockMain with side="start". Below 42rem of its own width (another width with `stackBelow`) the panel and splitter are hidden and DockBar shows at the bottom: open the panel's content in a bottom-sheet from `onOpenStacked`. Where the content ends in a region that must stay lowest (a composer), put a second DockBar inside DockMain above that region with `show="stacked"`, and give the one after the panel `show="collapsed"`. Give the Dock a height (it fills its parent).

```tsx
<Dock defaultSize={32} minSize={24} maxSize={50} className="h-[32rem]">
  <DockMain>…the conversation…</DockMain>
  <DockResizer aria-label="Resize the plan" />
  <DockPanel aria-label="Plan">
    <DockCollapse aria-label="Hide the plan"><PanelRightClose /></DockCollapse>
    …the plan…
  </DockPanel>
  <DockBar onOpenStacked={() => setSheetOpen(true)}>Plan · 3 stops</DockBar>
</Dock>

// Controlled, in pixels, at the start
<Dock side="start" unit="px" size={width} onSizeChange={setWidth} minSize={240} maxSize={480} collapsed={hidden} onCollapsedChange={setHidden}>…</Dock>

// Stacks below 56rem; on a narrow dock the bar sits above the composer, not under it
<Dock stackBelow={56} className="h-[32rem]">
  <DockMain className="flex flex-col">
    <div className="min-h-0 flex-1 overflow-y-auto">…the conversation…</div>
    <DockBar show="stacked" onOpenStacked={() => setSheetOpen(true)}>Plan · 3 stops</DockBar>
    <footer>…the composer…</footer>
  </DockMain>
  <DockResizer aria-label="Resize the plan" />
  <DockPanel aria-label="Plan">…</DockPanel>
  <DockBar show="collapsed">Plan · 3 stops</DockBar>
</Dock>
```

### dropdown-menu

A menu of actions that opens from a button: items, checkbox and radio items, labels, separators, sub-menus and a shortcut slot.

Use it: A list of actions or options behind one button (an account menu, "more" on a row). For choosing one value in a form use select; for actions on right-click use context-menu; for free content use popover. An icon-only trigger needs an `aria-label`.

```tsx
<DropdownMenu>
  <DropdownMenuTrigger asChild><Button variant="outline">Options</Button></DropdownMenuTrigger>
  <DropdownMenuContent align="start">
    <DropdownMenuLabel>Project</DropdownMenuLabel>
    <DropdownMenuItem>Rename <DropdownMenuShortcut>F2</DropdownMenuShortcut></DropdownMenuItem>
    <DropdownMenuCheckboxItem checked>Show in sidebar</DropdownMenuCheckboxItem>
    <DropdownMenuSub>
      <DropdownMenuSubTrigger>Move to</DropdownMenuSubTrigger>
      <DropdownMenuSubContent>
        <DropdownMenuRadioGroup value="work">
          <DropdownMenuRadioItem value="work">Work</DropdownMenuRadioItem>
          <DropdownMenuRadioItem value="archive">Archive</DropdownMenuRadioItem>
        </DropdownMenuRadioGroup>
      </DropdownMenuSubContent>
    </DropdownMenuSub>
    <DropdownMenuSeparator />
    <DropdownMenuItem variant="destructive">Delete</DropdownMenuItem>
  </DropdownMenuContent>
</DropdownMenu>
```

### dropzone

A place to choose files to upload, by dropping them, pasting them or pressing a button, and the rows that show each file's progress with slots for pause, resume, retry and remove.

Use it: Adding pictures, documents or other files where progress matters: a listing's photos, attachments, an import. It contains no upload engine: the project uploads (plain, or resumable such as tus) and tells each row its state and progress. For one small file in a form, an input with type="file" is enough. Name the dropzone with `aria-label` or `aria-labelledby`, and word rejected files yourself from the reason given to `onReject`.

```tsx
<Dropzone accept="image/*" maxSize={10_000_000} onFiles={start} onReject={explain} aria-label="Add pictures">
  <DropzoneHint>Drop pictures here, or</DropzoneHint>
  <DropzoneButton>Choose pictures</DropzoneButton>
</Dropzone>
<UploadList aria-label="Pictures being added">
  {uploads.map((upload) => (
    <UploadItem key={upload.id} name={upload.file.name} size={upload.file.size} state={upload.state}>
      <UploadProgress value={upload.percent} />
      <UploadActions>
        {upload.state === "uploading" ? <UploadPause onClick={() => pause(upload.id)} /> : null}
        {upload.state === "paused" ? <UploadResume onClick={() => resume(upload.id)} /> : null}
        {upload.state === "failed" ? <UploadRetry onClick={() => retry(upload.id)} /> : null}
        <UploadRemove onClick={() => remove(upload.id)} />
      </UploadActions>
    </UploadItem>
  ))}
</UploadList>

// A state of the project's own, with its word and tone; and a row that is not a list item
<UploadItem as="div" name="walk.mp4" state="checking" stateLabel="Being checked" stateTone="warning" />
```

### empty-state

What a list, a table or a search shows when there is nothing in it: an icon, a title, a description and an action.

Use it: An empty list, zero search results, a first run. Say what belongs here and offer the one action that fills it. For a failure use alert; while loading use skeleton.

```tsx
<EmptyState
  title="No projects yet"
  description="Projects you create will appear here."
  action={<Button>New project</Button>}
/>
<EmptyState icon={<SearchX />} title="No results" description="Try a shorter search." bordered={false} />
```

### fact-row

One thing the system knows or remembers about a person or a record, shown with where it came from and what the person can do about it: correct it in place, say it is no longer true, or have it removed.

Use it: Showing people what is held about them and letting them control it: remembered preferences, profile details filled in by an assistant, imported data, settings inferred from use. Every fact gets a source and at least one action. The words of the actions are the project's (the component names none). For plain label and value pairs nobody can change use a description list; for a form use field.

```tsx
<FactList aria-label="What we remember">
  <FactRow removed={forgotten} removedMessage="Diet was forgotten" restoredMessage="Diet was restored">
    <FactLabel>Diet</FactLabel>
    <FactValue>{diet}</FactValue>
    <FactSource>
      <SourceChip icon={<MessageSquare />}>You said this on 3 May</SourceChip>
    </FactSource>
    <FactActions aria-label="Diet">
      <FactEditTrigger>Edit</FactEditTrigger>
      <FactAction onClick={endDiet}>Not true any more</FactAction>
      <FactAction onClick={() => setForgotten(true)}>Forget this</FactAction>
    </FactActions>
    <FactEditor aria-label="Diet" defaultValue={diet} onSave={setDiet} savedMessage="Diet was changed" />
    <FactRemoved>
      Diet was forgotten. <FactUndo onClick={() => setForgotten(false)}>Undo</FactUndo>
    </FactRemoved>
  </FactRow>
</FactList>
```

### field

Lays out a label, a control, a description and an error message, and connects them (htmlFor, id, aria-describedby, aria-invalid) without hand-written ids.

Use it: Every control in a form. Put the control inside FieldControl; render FieldError only when there is a message and the field turns invalid by itself. Use orientation="horizontal" for a checkbox or switch beside its label, and FieldControl group for a radio group, toggle group or slider.

```tsx
<Field>
  <FieldLabel>Email</FieldLabel>
  <FieldControl><Input type="email" /></FieldControl>
  <FieldDescription>We only use it to reply.</FieldDescription>
  <FieldError>{error}</FieldError>
</Field>
<Field orientation="horizontal">
  <FieldControl><Switch /></FieldControl>
  <FieldLabel>Weekly summary</FieldLabel>
</Field>
<Field>
  <FieldLabel>Plan</FieldLabel>
  <FieldControl group>
    <RadioGroup defaultValue="pro">
      <Label><RadioGroupItem value="free" /> Free</Label>
      <Label><RadioGroupItem value="pro" /> Pro</Label>
    </RadioGroup>
  </FieldControl>
</Field>
```

### gallery

A set of picture tiles that open a full-screen viewer: a mosaic of one large and several small, an even grid, or a row that scrolls sideways.

Use it: Showing several pictures of one thing where each can be looked at closely: a place, a product, a piece of work. GalleryLightbox takes a list of pictures and does everything; Gallery, GalleryItem and GalleryImage are the parts, to put inside your own Lightbox or to use with no viewer at all. Pictures are plain `<img>` elements unless the project gives its framework's image component: `as` on GalleryImage, `renderImage` on GalleryLightbox. For pictures that are decoration, use plain images in a grid; for one picture use aspect.

```tsx
<GalleryLightbox
  title="Photos of the studio"
  layout="mosaic"
  items={[
    { src: "/studio-1.jpg", alt: "The studio from the street" },
    { src: "/studio-2.jpg", alt: "The workbench", caption: "The workbench, built in 1962" },
  ]}
/>

// The parts, in your own lightbox
<Lightbox count={photos.length}>
  <Gallery layout="grid" aria-label="Photos">
    {photos.map((photo, index) => (
      <LightboxTrigger key={photo.src} index={index} asChild>
        <GalleryItem><GalleryImage src={photo.src} alt={photo.alt} /></GalleryItem>
      </LightboxTrigger>
    ))}
  </Gallery>
  <LightboxContent>…</LightboxContent>
</Lightbox>

// With the framework's image component (here next/image) in place of <img>
<GalleryImage as={Image} fill sizes="(min-width: 48rem) 25vw, 50vw" src={photo.src} alt={photo.alt} />
<GalleryLightbox
  title="Photos of the studio"
  items={photos}
  renderImage={({ use, picture, props }) =>
    use === "tile" ? <GalleryImage as={Image} fill sizes="25vw" {...props} /> : <Image {...props} width={use === "slide" ? picture.width : 96} height={use === "slide" ? picture.height : 72} />
  }
/>
```

### hotspots

Named buttons placed over a picture or a video at a point, each present only between two moments of the clip, with the same choices as a plain list for people who cannot point at the picture.

Use it: Something in the frame can be asked about or chosen while it is on screen: an object in a scene, a place on a still, a choice in a story. Put Hotspots inside the frame (VideoPlayer, or any `relative` box over a picture) and HotspotList after it; both take the same `hotspots`. A hotspot that appears is announced, because nothing else would tell a screen-reader user it is there. For a point on a map use the map's own markers; for marks on the time bar use the scrubber's `marks`.

```tsx
const spots = [
  { id: "kiln", x: 32, y: 55, start: 4, end: 12, label: "The kiln door" },
  { id: "shelf", x: 70, y: 30, start: 9, end: 20, label: "Drying shelf" },
];
<VideoPlayerProvider>
  <VideoPlayer aria-label="Inside the workshop">
    <VideoPlayerVideo src="/workshop.mp4" />
    <Hotspots hotspots={spots} onSelect={(spot) => openCard(spot.id)} />
    <VideoPlayerControls>…</VideoPlayerControls>
  </VideoPlayer>
  <HotspotList hotspots={spots} onSelect={(spot) => openCard(spot.id)} aria-label="In this scene" />
</VideoPlayerProvider>
```

### input-group

An input with a leading or trailing icon, text or button inside one shared border.

Use it: A search box with an icon, a URL with a fixed prefix, a field with a unit or an inline action. For a plain input use input. Inside a field, wrap InputGroupInput (not the group) in FieldControl.

```tsx
<InputGroup>
  <InputGroupAddon><Search strokeWidth={1.5} /></InputGroupAddon>
  <InputGroupInput type="search" placeholder="Search" aria-label="Search" />
</InputGroup>
<InputGroup size="sm">
  <InputGroupAddon>https://</InputGroupAddon>
  <InputGroupInput placeholder="example.com" aria-label="Website" />
  <InputGroupAddon><InputGroupButton>Check</InputGroupButton></InputGroupAddon>
</InputGroup>
```

### input

A single-line text input in three sizes, with an invalid state.

Use it: Short free text: a name, an email, a number. Wrap it in field for a label and an error; use textarea for several lines, select for a fixed list, input-group to add an icon or a button inside the edge.

```tsx
<Input type="email" placeholder="you@example.com" />
<Input size="sm" defaultValue="Rivier" />
<Input aria-invalid="true" aria-label="Email" defaultValue="not-an-email" />
```

### kbd

A key cap for showing a keyboard key or a shortcut.

Use it: Naming a key the reader can press: in a menu item, a tooltip, a hint under a field. Wrap a combination in KbdGroup, one Kbd per key.

```tsx
<Kbd>Esc</Kbd>
<KbdGroup>
  <Kbd>Ctrl</Kbd>
  <Kbd>K</Kbd>
</KbdGroup>
```

### label

The text name of a control. Clicking it focuses or toggles the control it points to.

Use it: Every control needs one. Point it at a control with htmlFor, or wrap a checkbox, radio or switch in it so the whole row is the hit area. Inside field, use FieldLabel, which wires htmlFor for you.

```tsx
<Label htmlFor="email">Email</Label>
<Input id="email" type="email" />
<Label><Checkbox /> Remember me</Label>
```

### language-switcher

A menu for choosing the interface language: each language under its own name in its own script, the current one marked, no flags.

Use it: A product in more than one language: in the header or footer, and in settings. It only reports the choice (`onValueChange`): the project navigates to the translated page or stores the preference. A flag stands for a country, not a language, so none is shown. It is a menu of radio items and not a select, because choosing a language is an action that reloads or navigates: a select that changes the page as its value changes surprises keyboard and screen-reader users. For choosing a language as data in a form (a document's language) use select.

```tsx
<LanguageSwitcher value={locale} onValueChange={(next) => router.replace(pathname, { locale: next })} label="Language" languages={["en", "fr", "ar", "ja"]} />

// With its own parts: names in the current language as a second line, and a name the project supplies
<LanguageSwitcher defaultValue="en" label="Language" displayLocale="en">
  <LanguageSwitcherTrigger />
  <LanguageSwitcherContent align="end">
    <LanguageSwitcherItem value="en" />
    <LanguageSwitcherItem value="ar" />
    <LanguageSwitcherItem value="dv" name="ދިވެހި" />
  </LanguageSwitcherContent>
</LanguageSwitcher>
```

### lightbox

A full-screen viewer for a set of pictures (or any media the project renders): swipe or arrow between slides, zoom and pan, a counter, captions, thumbnails, and the picture growing out of the thumbnail that opened it.

Use it: Looking closely at pictures that are shown small on the page: a listing's photos, a portfolio, attachments. It is a modal dialog, so focus is held inside and returns to the thumbnail of the picture shown when it closes. For a grid of thumbnails that opens it use gallery (GalleryLightbox does both). For one picture with text beside it use dialog; for a row of cards that scroll in the page use a scroll-snap row, not a lightbox. Always give it a LightboxTitle (className="sr-only" hides it) and say how many slides there are with `count`.

```tsx
<Lightbox count={photos.length}>
  {photos.map((photo, index) => (
    <LightboxTrigger key={photo.src} index={index} aria-label={`Open picture: ${photo.alt}`}>
      <img src={photo.thumb} alt="" className="size-24 rounded-control object-cover" />
    </LightboxTrigger>
  ))}
  <LightboxContent>
    <LightboxHeader>
      <LightboxTitle className="sr-only">Photos</LightboxTitle>
      <LightboxCounter />
      <LightboxZoom className="ms-auto" />
      <LightboxClose />
    </LightboxHeader>
    <LightboxStage>
      <LightboxViewport>
        {photos.map((photo, index) => (
          <LightboxSlide key={photo.src} index={index}>
            <img src={photo.src} alt={photo.alt} className="max-h-full max-w-full object-contain" />
          </LightboxSlide>
        ))}
      </LightboxViewport>
      <LightboxPrevious />
      <LightboxNext />
    </LightboxStage>
  </LightboxContent>
</Lightbox>
```

### media-row-list

The pictures or clips a person has added, as rows they can put in order, describe and choose a cover from: each row shows its state in words (an upload's, or one the project names), its progress or its error with pause, resume and retry, a field for its text alternative that can be required, a "cover" choice, a remove button, and room for a status line and controls of the project's own.

Use it: After a dropzone, when the order of the files matters and each needs a description: the photos of a listing, the slides of a story, the pages of a document. It is ready-made from sortable-list (drag by the handle, lift and move with the keyboard, or the move buttons; every move is read out) and the upload rows of dropzone, and contains no upload engine: the project uploads and passes each row its state. For files whose order does not matter use the dropzone's own UploadList; to reorder things that are not files use sortable-list.

```tsx
const [rows, setRows] = useState<MediaRow[]>([
  { id: "a", name: "kitchen.jpg", size: 1_200_000, state: "done", alt: "The kitchen, from the door" },
  { id: "b", name: "garden.jpg", size: 2_400_000, state: "uploading", progress: 40 },
  { id: "c", name: "stairs.jpg", state: "failed", error: "The connection dropped." },
]);
const [cover, setCover] = useState<string | null>("a");
<MediaRowList
  aria-label="Pictures, in order"
  items={rows}
  onItemsChange={setRows}
  cover={cover}
  onCoverChange={setCover}
  onAltChange={(id, alt) => setRows((all) => all.map((row) => (row.id === id ? { ...row, alt } : row)))}
  onRemove={(id) => setRows((all) => all.filter((row) => row.id !== id))}
  onRetry={(id) => upload(id)}
/>

// A state of the project's own, a status line, a control of its own, no cover choice, and a description that is required
const row: MediaRow = {
  id: "d", name: "walk.mp4", state: "checking", stateLabel: "Being checked", stateTone: "warning",
  status: "Usually takes a minute.", controls: <Button size="sm" variant="ghost">Trim</Button>,
  hideCover: true, altRequired: true, altError: "Say what the clip shows.",
};
<MediaRowList aria-label="Clips" items={[row]} variant="lines" onAltChange={describe} onPause={pause} onResume={resume} onDropped={({ values }) => save(values)} />
```

### message

One message in a conversation, from the person, the assistant or the system, with parts for an avatar, the words, the time and sending state, a toolbar of actions, and suggested replies.

Use it: Inside a thread, one per message. The person's own messages sit at the end side in a bubble; the assistant's read as plain text at the start. For words that are still arriving put streaming-text inside MessageContent; for a structured piece of a reply (a plan, a form) use part-frame beside it. Not for comments under an article or a notification list: those are plain lists.

```tsx
<Message from="user">
  <MessageBody>
    <MessageContent>Somewhere quiet for lunch on Saturday?</MessageContent>
    <MessageMeta time={sentAt} status="failed" />
  </MessageBody>
</Message>

<Message from="assistant">
  <MessageAvatar><Avatar size="sm"><AvatarFallback>AI</AvatarFallback></Avatar></MessageAvatar>
  <MessageBody>
    <MessageContent>Three places are open then.</MessageContent>
    <MessageActions aria-label="Actions for this reply">
      <MessageAction aria-label="Copy" onClick={copy}><Copy /></MessageAction>
      <MessageAction aria-label="Try again" onClick={retry}><RotateCcw /></MessageAction>
    </MessageActions>
    <MessageSuggestions aria-label="Suggested replies">
      <MessageSuggestion onClick={() => send("Only outdoors")}>Only outdoors</MessageSuggestion>
    </MessageSuggestions>
  </MessageBody>
</Message>
```

### navbar

A responsive site header: a brand, a row of links and a slot for actions. Below `md` the links move into a menu button that opens them in a sheet.

Use it: The top of a site or app with up to about seven top-level links. The links are written once, as NavbarLink children, and shown in the bar or in the sheet. The sheet closes when a link in it is followed, and focus returns to the menu button. Mark the current page with `current`. With a router link, pass it through `asChild`. For navigation inside a page use tabs; for the path to a page use breadcrumb.

```tsx
<Navbar
  brand={<a href="/" className="text-base font-medium">Rivier</a>}
  actions={<Button size="sm" asChild><a href="/contact">Contact</a></Button>}
>
  <NavbarLink href="/work" current>Work</NavbarLink>
  <NavbarLink href="/studio">Studio</NavbarLink>
  <NavbarLink href="/about">About</NavbarLink>
</Navbar>
```

### number-stepper

A number with a button either side to take one away or add one, that can also be typed: a spin button.

Use it: A small whole number that is usually changed by a step or two: people in a party, a quantity, nights. For a number where the rough position matters use slider; for a free number (a price, a year) use input with type="number". Name it with a Label (pass the same `id`) or `aria-label`.

```tsx
<Label htmlFor="adults">Adults</Label>
<NumberStepper id="adults" defaultValue={2} min={1} max={12} />

// Controlled, with its own parts and translated button names
<NumberStepper value={nights} onValueChange={setNights} min={1} aria-label="Nights">
  <NumberStepperDecrement aria-label="One night fewer" />
  <NumberStepperInput />
  <NumberStepperIncrement aria-label="One night more" />
</NumberStepper>
```

### pagination

Links to the previous, next and numbered pages of a long list, with the look of buttons.

Use it: A list or table split over pages that people may want to jump within or link to. Each page is a real link, so it works without JavaScript; with a router link, pass it through `asChild`. On the first or last page give PaginationPrevious or PaginationNext `aria-disabled="true"` and no `href`. For a feed with no natural page numbers use a "Load more" button.

```tsx
<Pagination>
  <PaginationContent>
    <PaginationItem><PaginationPrevious href="?page=1" /></PaginationItem>
    <PaginationItem><PaginationLink href="?page=1">1</PaginationLink></PaginationItem>
    <PaginationItem><PaginationLink href="?page=2" isActive>2</PaginationLink></PaginationItem>
    <PaginationItem><PaginationEllipsis /></PaginationItem>
    <PaginationItem><PaginationLink href="?page=9">9</PaginationLink></PaginationItem>
    <PaginationItem><PaginationNext href="?page=3" /></PaginationItem>
  </PaginationContent>
</Pagination>
```

### part-frame

A card for one structured piece of a conversation (a plan, a result, a form) that has a life: loading, live, saving a change, replaced by a newer one, or final.

Use it: An assistant's reply contains something to look at or work in, not only words, and that thing changes over the conversation. The frame holds its size while it loads, says "Saving" in words while a change is on its way, shrinks to a one-line stub when a newer frame replaces it, and can open its content full screen. For a static card use card; for words use message; for a flow of steps put steps or a wizard inside it.

```tsx
<PartFrame state={plan.state} replacementRef={newerPlan}>
  <PartFrameHeader>
    <PartFrameTitle>Plan for Saturday</PartFrameTitle>
    <PartFrameExpand title="Plan for Saturday"><PlanEditor plan={plan} roomy /></PartFrameExpand>
  </PartFrameHeader>
  <PartFrameContent className="min-h-40"><PlanEditor plan={plan} /></PartFrameContent>
  <PartFrameFooter><Button size="sm">Confirm</Button></PartFrameFooter>
</PartFrame>

// Replaced by a newer one: a stub that says so and points to it
<PartFrame state="superseded" supersededBy={<a href="#plan-2">See the new plan</a>}>
  <PartFrameHeader><PartFrameTitle>Plan for Saturday</PartFrameTitle></PartFrameHeader>
  <PartFrameContent>…</PartFrameContent>
</PartFrame>
```

### popover

A small floating surface attached to the control that opens it.

Use it: Extra controls or details that belong to one control: a date picker, a share box, quick settings. For a hint of a few words use tooltip; for a list of actions use dropdown-menu; for a task that must block the page use dialog.

```tsx
<Popover>
  <PopoverTrigger asChild><Button variant="outline">Share</Button></PopoverTrigger>
  <PopoverContent align="start">
    <p className="text-sm font-medium">Share this page</p>
    <p className="text-sm text-muted-foreground">Anyone with the link can view it.</p>
  </PopoverContent>
</Popover>
```

### price-breakdown

What a price is made of, line by line, and the total: labels at the start, amounts in aligned figures at the end.

Use it: A quote, a basket summary, a receipt, a booking's cost before paying. Every amount the total includes gets a line, discounts and fees too. For one figure with a label use stat; for many records in rows and columns use table.

```tsx
<PriceBreakdown currency="EUR" locale="en-IE" announceTotal={(total) => `Total is now ${total}`}>
  <PriceLine label="2 adults" note="€46 each" amount={92} />
  <PriceLine label="Service fee" amount={6} />
  <PriceLine label="Early booking" amount={-10} discount />
  <PriceTotal label="Total" note="Taxes included" amount={88} />
</PriceBreakdown>
```

### progress

A bar that fills as a task completes, or slides back and forth when the amount done is not known.

Use it: A wait that can be measured: an upload, a multi-step job. Leave `value` out (or pass null) for the indeterminate state. For a short unknown wait use spinner. Always label it.

```tsx
<Progress value={64} aria-label="Uploading" />
<Progress value={3} max={8} size="sm" aria-label="Step 3 of 8" />
<Progress aria-label="Connecting" />
```

### provenance-label

A label that stays on a picture, a video or a 3D view and says what it is (a photograph, a reconstruction, made by a model), with a popover for its sources, placed so the media's own controls can never cover it.

Use it: A reader must not mistake what they are looking at: a reconstruction beside a photograph, a generated picture, an artist's impression, archive footage. Two placements. ProvenanceFrame puts the label in its own strip above the media, outside the media's box, where nothing the media draws can reach it: use this by default. `position` puts it over a top corner inside the media's box, above its controls and on a solid ground: use this when the label must also stay in full screen, with the label inside the element that goes full screen. The bottom edge is left to controls and captions. For the source of one fact in text use fact-row's SourceChip; for a key of classes inside a scene use certainty-legend.

```tsx
// In its own strip above the media
<ProvenanceFrame>
  <ProvenanceLabel details={<p>Drawn from the 1890 survey and two photographs. The roof is a guess.</p>}>Imagined reconstruction</ProvenanceLabel>
  <img src="/mill.jpg" alt="The mill as it may have looked" />
</ProvenanceFrame>

// Over a corner of a player, so it stays in full screen
<VideoPlayer aria-label="The mill, reconstructed">
  <VideoPlayerVideo src="/mill.mp4" />
  <ProvenanceLabel position="top-start">Imagined reconstruction</ProvenanceLabel>
  <VideoPlayerControls>…</VideoPlayerControls>
</VideoPlayer>
```

### radio-group

A set of radio buttons where exactly one is chosen, with arrow-key movement between them.

Use it: Picking one of two to five options that should all be visible. For a longer list use select; for a compact row of icons or short words use toggle-group; for on or off use switch.

```tsx
<RadioGroup defaultValue="monthly" aria-label="Billing period">
  <Label><RadioGroupItem value="monthly" /> Monthly</Label>
  <Label><RadioGroupItem value="yearly" /> Yearly</Label>
</RadioGroup>
```

### scene-strip

A row of the scenes or chapters of a clip, each with a picture, a name and a length, that scrolls sideways, marks the one that is playing and goes to a scene when it is pressed.

Use it: Under or beside a player whose clip has named parts: chapters of a lesson, scenes of a film, steps of a recipe. It reads the time from the player it is inside (wrap the player and the strip in VideoPlayerProvider, or put it inside AudioPlayer), or from `time` and `onSeek`. For marks on the time bar itself use the scrubber's `marks`; for the spoken lines use Transcript.

```tsx
<VideoPlayerProvider>
  <VideoPlayer aria-label="A day at the pottery">…</VideoPlayer>
  <SceneStrip
    aria-label="Scenes"
    scenes={[
      { start: 0, label: "Wedging the clay", picture: <img src="/scene-1.jpg" alt="" /> },
      { start: 42, label: "On the wheel", picture: <img src="/scene-2.jpg" alt="" /> },
    ]}
  />
</VideoPlayerProvider>
```

### scroll-area

A scrolling region with thin, themed scrollbars that look the same on every platform. Native scrolling underneath.

Use it: A bounded list or panel inside a surface: a menu, a sidebar, a log. Give it a height (or a max height). The page itself, and anything that can simply grow, should scroll natively.

```tsx
<ScrollArea className="h-64 rounded-surface border" aria-label="Changelog">
  <div className="p-4 text-sm">Long content…</div>
</ScrollArea>
<ScrollArea orientation="horizontal" className="w-full">
  <div className="flex w-max gap-3 pb-3">…</div>
</ScrollArea>
```

### scrubber

The time bar of a player: a slider over the length of a clip that shows what has played and what has loaded, marks chapters, and can show the time and a picture for the moment under the pointer.

Use it: Seeking in audio, video or any timeline measured in seconds. video-player and audio-player already contain one bound to their media; use this directly for a custom player or a timeline. For choosing a number that is not a time use slider. Time runs left to right in every language (as on players everywhere: the bar is a picture of time, like a clock face, not a line of text), so the bar and its arrow keys are not mirrored in right-to-left pages; pass `dir="rtl"` if a product decides otherwise, and the keys follow what is drawn.

```tsx
// Uncontrolled
<Scrubber duration={200} defaultValue={65} aria-label="Seek" onValueCommit={(time) => player.seek(time)} />

// Controlled by the player's clock, with chapters and a preview picture from a sprite sheet
<Scrubber
  value={time}
  duration={duration}
  buffered={[[0, 90]]}
  marks={[{ time: 0, label: "Opening" }, { time: 60, label: "The climb" }]}
  onValueCommit={seek}
  aria-label="Seek"
>
  <ScrubberTrack />
  <ScrubberThumb />
  <ScrubberPreview thumbnail={{ url: "/sprite.jpg", columns: 10, rows: 10, interval: 2 }} />
</Scrubber>
```

### segmented-control

A row of two to five segments where exactly one is chosen, with a marker that slides to the choice.

Use it: Switching one setting between a few short, equal options that take effect at once: a view (list or map), a unit, a period (day, week, month). It is a radio group, so one option is always chosen. For switching panels of content use tabs; for options that can each be on or off use toggle-group or chip; for more than five options use select.

```tsx
<SegmentedControl defaultValue="list" aria-label="View">
  <SegmentedControlItem value="list">List</SegmentedControlItem>
  <SegmentedControlItem value="map">Map</SegmentedControlItem>
</SegmentedControl>

// Controlled, full width, with icons
<SegmentedControl value={period} onValueChange={setPeriod} aria-label="Period" className="w-full">
  <SegmentedControlItem value="day"><Sun /> Day</SegmentedControlItem>
  <SegmentedControlItem value="week"><Calendar /> Week</SegmentedControlItem>
</SegmentedControl>
```

### select

A themed dropdown for choosing one value from a list, with groups, labels and separators. Never a native select.

Use it: Picking one of more than about five options, or when space is tight. For two to five visible options use radio-group; for a short row of icons use toggle-group.

```tsx
<Select defaultValue="eur">
  <SelectTrigger aria-label="Currency" className="w-48">
    <SelectValue placeholder="Currency" />
  </SelectTrigger>
  <SelectContent>
    <SelectGroup>
      <SelectLabel>Europe</SelectLabel>
      <SelectItem value="eur">Euro</SelectItem>
      <SelectItem value="sek">Swedish krona</SelectItem>
    </SelectGroup>
    <SelectSeparator />
    <SelectGroup>
      <SelectLabel>Americas</SelectLabel>
      <SelectItem value="usd">US dollar</SelectItem>
      <SelectItem value="cad" disabled>Canadian dollar</SelectItem>
    </SelectGroup>
  </SelectContent>
</Select>
```

### separator

A hairline between two pieces of content, horizontal or vertical, with an optional label in the middle.

Use it: Dividing groups inside a surface or a toolbar. Between page sections use section spacing instead, and inside a list prefer a border on the rows.

```tsx
<Separator />
<Separator>or continue with</Separator>
<div className="flex h-5 items-center gap-3">
  <span>Docs</span>
  <Separator orientation="vertical" />
  <span>Blog</span>
</div>
```

### sheet

A modal panel that slides in from an edge of the screen, with parts for a header, title, description and footer.

Use it: Navigation, filters, details or a longer form beside the page. `side` is "end" by default ("start" and "end" follow the reading direction; "left" and "right" do not); on phones "bottom" is the natural choice, because it is within reach of the thumb. For a short decision in the middle of the screen use dialog. Always give it a SheetTitle (add className="sr-only" to hide it). Opened by state with no SheetTrigger, focus does not return on close: remember the opener (`opener.current = document.activeElement`) and refocus it in `onCloseAutoFocus={(event) => { event.preventDefault(); opener.current?.focus(); }}` on SheetContent.

```tsx
<Sheet>
  <SheetTrigger asChild><Button variant="outline">Filters</Button></SheetTrigger>
  <SheetContent side="bottom">
    <SheetHeader>
      <SheetTitle>Filters</SheetTitle>
      <SheetDescription>Narrow the list of projects.</SheetDescription>
    </SheetHeader>
    <div className="px-5">…</div>
    <SheetFooter>
      <SheetClose asChild><Button>Show results</Button></SheetClose>
    </SheetFooter>
  </SheetContent>
</Sheet>
```

### skeleton

A pulsing block that stands in for content that is loading: a bare block sized by hand, lines of text, or a wrapper that takes the exact size of the real content. It is still under reduced motion.

Use it: Content whose shape is known is on its way. Nothing may jump when it arrives: either size the block like the thing it replaces, or wrap the real component (rendered with placeholder data) in `<Skeleton loading>` so the box is exactly its final size. Mark the region that is loading with `aria-busy="true"`: the placeholders themselves are hidden from assistive technology. For an unknown wait use spinner; for a measurable one use progress.

```tsx
<div className="flex items-center gap-3" aria-busy="true">
  <Skeleton className="size-10 rounded-full" />
  <SkeletonText lines={2} className="flex-1" />
</div>

// Holds the final size: the card is laid out, invisible and inert, under the placeholder
<section aria-busy={isLoading}>
  <Skeleton loading={isLoading}>
    <PriceCard price={price ?? PLACEHOLDER_PRICE} />
  </Skeleton>
</section>
```

### slider

A slider for one value, or a range with two thumbs.

Use it: Choosing a number where the rough position matters more than the exact figure: volume, a price range. When the exact number matters use an input with type="number".

```tsx
<Slider defaultValue={[40]} max={100} step={5} aria-label="Volume" />
<Slider defaultValue={[200, 800]} min={0} max={1000} step={50} thumbLabels={["Lowest price", "Highest price"]} />
```

### slot-picker

Offered times as a set of pills to choose one from, optionally under named groups, each able to carry a note and to be unavailable for a stated reason.

Use it: The times are a short list that someone else decides: appointment slots, sittings, departures. One is chosen, so it is a radio group. For any time of the person's own choosing use time-picker; for more than about twenty slots, narrow them first (by day, by part of the day) or use select.

```tsx
<SlotPicker defaultValue="10:00" aria-label="Time" locale="en-GB">
  <SlotPickerGroup label="Morning">
    <SlotPickerItem value="09:30" />
    <SlotPickerItem value="10:00" note="2 places left" />
    <SlotPickerItem value="11:30" unavailable="Full" />
  </SlotPickerGroup>
  <SlotPickerGroup label="Afternoon">
    <SlotPickerItem value="14:00" />
  </SlotPickerGroup>
</SlotPicker>

// Controlled, with its own labels, and nothing on offer
<SlotPicker value={slot} onValueChange={setSlot} aria-label="Sitting">
  {sittings.length === 0 ? <SlotPickerEmpty>Nothing is open on this day.</SlotPickerEmpty> : null}
  {sittings.map((sitting) => <SlotPickerItem key={sitting.id} value={sitting.id}>{sitting.name}</SlotPickerItem>)}
</SlotPicker>
```

### sortable-list

A list whose order the person sets, three ways: dragging a row by its handle (mouse, pen or touch), lifting it with the keyboard and moving it with the arrow keys, or pressing "Move up" and "Move down" buttons. Every move is read out.

Use it: The order itself is the data: the stops of a plan, priorities, pictures in a gallery, columns to show. Always give the rows SortableMoveButtons or a SortableHandle (both is best): dragging alone leaves out people who cannot drag (WCAG 2.5.7). It is one vertical list; it does not move rows between lists or sort a grid. For a list sorted by a rule (newest first) use a select for the rule instead; for choosing rather than ordering use chip or checkboxes.

```tsx
const [stops, setStops] = useState(["market", "lunch", "museum"]);
<SortableList values={stops} onValuesChange={setStops} aria-label="Stops, in order">
  {stops.map((id) => (
    <SortableItem key={id} value={id} label={NAMES[id]}>
      <SortableHandle />
      <span className="min-w-0 flex-1 truncate">{NAMES[id]}</span>
      <SortableMoveButtons />
    </SortableItem>
  ))}
</SortableList>

// Uncontrolled: the list keeps the order and gives it to its children
<SortableList defaultValues={["a", "b", "c"]} aria-label="Priorities">
  {(order) => order.map((id) => <SortableItem key={id} value={id} label={id}>…</SortableItem>)}
</SortableList>

// Save once, when a row has been let go, not at every step it passes
<SortableList values={stops} onValuesChange={setStops} onDropped={({ from, to, values }) => (from === to ? undefined : save(values))} aria-label="Stops, in order">…</SortableList>
```

### spinner

A turning ring that says something is in progress, announced to assistive technology by its label.

Use it: A short wait of unknown length. Inside a button use the button's `loading` prop; when the shape of the content is known use skeleton; when the amount done is known use progress.

```tsx
<Spinner />
<Spinner size="lg" label="Loading projects" />
<p className="flex items-center gap-2"><Spinner size="sm" label="Saving" /> Saving</p>
```

### stat

A number tile: a label, a value, an optional change with its direction, and a slot for a sparkline.

Use it: A headline figure on a dashboard or in a bento cell. Pass `change` as a magnitude ("12%"): the sign and the arrow are added from `direction`. For several figures compared over time use a chart or a table.

```tsx
<Stat label="Revenue" value="€48,200" change="12%" direction="up" changeLabel="vs last month" />
<Stat label="Churn" value="2.1%" change="0.4 pts" direction="up" tone="negative" />
<Stat
  label="Uptime"
  value="99.98%"
  chart={
    <svg viewBox="0 0 100 24" preserveAspectRatio="none" className="h-8 w-full" aria-hidden="true">
      <polyline points="0,18 20,14 40,16 60,8 80,10 100,4" fill="none" strokeWidth="1.5" className="stroke-chart-1" />
    </svg>
  }
/>
```

### status-line

One line that says in words what is happening now ("Searching", "Writing a reply", "Done"), read out politely by screen readers, with an optional moving mark and a slot for a stop button.

Use it: Beside a thread or any surface where work goes on that the person waits for: it is the one polite live region of that surface. Render it from the start, empty, and change its text: a region that appears together with its text is often not announced. It keeps its height when empty, so nothing jumps. For a wait with no words use spinner; for a measurable one use progress; for a result that must outlive the moment use alert or toaster.

```tsx
<StatusLine working={busy} action={busy ? <StatusLineAction onClick={stop}>Stop</StatusLineAction> : null}>
  {busy ? "Searching three sources" : ""}
</StatusLine>
```

### steps

A rail that shows where one is in a sequence of steps: a row of thin segments, or numbered markers with titles, each step with a state (done, filled in for you, current, not started, skipped, blocked).

Use it: Showing progress through a known, ordered set of steps: a booking, a sign-up, an import, a checklist that runs in order. Use "segments" above a card where space is short and "labelled" where the step names help. Pair it with StepsCount ("Step 2 of 5"), which says the same in words. For a measured amount of one task use progress; for the whole guided task with its buttons use wizard, which draws this rail itself; for moving between unordered views use tabs.

```tsx
<StepsCount current={2} total={4} />
<Steps aria-label="Booking progress">
  <Step state="done">Dates</Step>
  <Step state="current">People</Step>
  <Step state="upcoming">Extras</Step>
  <Step state="upcoming">Review</Step>
</Steps>

// Numbered markers with titles; a finished step can be a button that goes back to it
<Steps variant="labelled" aria-label="Import">
  <Step state="done" onClick={() => goTo("file")}>Choose a file</Step>
  <Step state="assumed" note="Taken from the file's first row">Match the columns</Step>
  <Step state="current" description="About a minute">Check the rows</Step>
  <Step state="skipped">Add notes</Step>
</Steps>
```

### streaming-text

Text that grows as it arrives, with a caret while it is arriving, that is never read out word by word: it is announced once, when it is finished.

Use it: A reply from a model, a transcript or a log line that streams in. Pass the text so far and whether more is coming. It must not sit inside a live region (a thread is `aria-live="off"`); say "Writing a reply" through a status-line while it streams. For text that is already complete use a plain element; for a headline that animates in use text-reveal.

```tsx
<MessageContent>
  <StreamingText text={reply} streaming={isStreaming} announceWhenDone onDone={saveReply} />
</MessageContent>

// A shorter spoken form, and words that fade in as they land
<StreamingText text={reply} streaming={isStreaming} reveal="word" announceWhenDone="Three places found. The nearest is ten minutes away." />

// The project's own renderer (Markdown, for example)
```
