```tsx
<StreamingText text={reply} streaming={isStreaming}>{(text) => <Markdown>{text}</Markdown>}</StreamingText>
```

### switch

An on/off switch.

Use it: A setting that takes effect as soon as it is flipped. For a choice that is submitted with a form use checkbox; for a pressed/unpressed toolbar button use toggle.

```tsx
<Label><Switch defaultChecked /> Weekly summary</Label>
<Switch aria-label="Dark mode" checked={dark} onCheckedChange={setDark} />
```

### table

A semantic table with styled parts, inside a wrapper that scrolls sideways so it never overflows a narrow screen.

Use it: Rows of the same kind of thing compared across columns. For sorting, filtering and paging build on these parts. For two or three facts per item use cards; for one number use stat.

```tsx
<Table>
  <TableCaption>Invoices this quarter</TableCaption>
  <TableHeader>
    <TableRow>
      <TableHead>Invoice</TableHead>
      <TableHead>Status</TableHead>
      <TableHead numeric>Amount</TableHead>
    </TableRow>
  </TableHeader>
  <TableBody>
    <TableRow>
      <TableCell>INV-001</TableCell>
      <TableCell>Paid</TableCell>
      <TableCell numeric>€250.00</TableCell>
    </TableRow>
  </TableBody>
  <TableFooter>
    <TableRow>
      <TableCell colSpan={2}>Total</TableCell>
      <TableCell numeric>€250.00</TableCell>
    </TableRow>
  </TableFooter>
</Table>
```

### tabs

Panels that share one place, switched by a row of tabs. Two looks: an underline, or a segmented pill.

Use it: Views of the same thing that people switch between without leaving the page. `variant="underline"` (the default) for sections of a page; `variant="pill"` for a compact switch between two to four views. For moving between pages use links (navbar, breadcrumb); for stacked sections that can be open together use accordion.

```tsx
<Tabs defaultValue="overview">
  <TabsList aria-label="Project">
    <TabsTrigger value="overview">Overview</TabsTrigger>
    <TabsTrigger value="activity">Activity</TabsTrigger>
  </TabsList>
  <TabsContent value="overview">The overview.</TabsContent>
  <TabsContent value="activity">The activity.</TabsContent>
</Tabs>

<Tabs defaultValue="month">
  <TabsList variant="pill" aria-label="Billing period">
    <TabsTrigger value="month">Monthly</TabsTrigger>
    <TabsTrigger value="year">Yearly</TabsTrigger>
  </TabsList>
  <TabsContent value="month">Billed every month.</TabsContent>
  <TabsContent value="year">Billed once a year.</TabsContent>
</Tabs>
```

### textarea

A multi-line text input that grows with its content, with an invalid state.

Use it: Free text of more than one line: a message, a note, a description. Wrap it in field for a label and an error; use input for a single line.

```tsx
<Textarea placeholder="Tell us about the project" rows={4} />
<Textarea aria-invalid="true" aria-label="Message" defaultValue="Too short" />
```

### theme-provider

Holds the theme (light or dark, roundness, highlight colour), applies it to the page, remembers the visitor's choice, and avoids a flash of the wrong theme.

Use it: Once, around the app in the root layout, when visitors or the product can change the theme. For a fixed theme, skip it and set the attributes on <html> by hand.

```tsx
// app/layout.tsx
<html lang="en" suppressHydrationWarning>
  <head><ThemeScript defaults={{ mode: "system", radius: "md", accent: "blue" }} /></head>
  <body>
    <ThemeProvider defaults={{ mode: "system", radius: "md", accent: "blue" }}>{children}</ThemeProvider>
  </body>
</html>

// anywhere below
const { theme, setTheme } = useTheme();
setTheme({ mode: "dark" });
setTheme({ accent: { hue: 262, chroma: 0.19 } });
```

### thread

The scrolling log of a conversation: it follows the newest content while the person is at the bottom, stops the moment they scroll up, and offers a way back down.

Use it: A conversation with an assistant or between people, where messages arrive over time. It holds no messages and no transport: render them inside it (message, streaming-text, part-frame). The log is deliberately silent (`aria-live="off"`): say what is happening through one status-line beside it, and the finished reply once through streaming-text's `announceWhenDone`. For a list that does not grow at the bottom use scroll-area.

```tsx
<Thread aria-label="Conversation with the assistant" className="h-[32rem]">
  <ThreadContent>
    {messages.length === 0 ? <ThreadEmpty>Ask anything to begin.</ThreadEmpty> : null}
    {messages.map((message) => (
      <ThreadTurn key={message.id} label={message.from === "user" ? "You" : "Assistant"}>
        <Message from={message.from}>
          <MessageBody><MessageContent>{message.text}</MessageContent></MessageBody>
        </Message>
      </ThreadTurn>
    ))}
  </ThreadContent>
  <ThreadJump>Jump to latest</ThreadJump>
</Thread>

// Always show what the person just sent, even if they had scrolled up
<Thread aria-label="Conversation" resumeKey={lastOwnMessageId}>…</Thread>
```

### tile-group

A grid of large tiles, each a picture or an icon with a word, where one or several are chosen.

Use it: A choice that is easier to make by looking than by reading: moods, styles, room types, plans. Each tile must carry a visible word; the picture alone is never the label. For short text-only options use chip (ChipGroup); for a compact switch between a few views use segmented-control; for a long list use select or combobox.

```tsx
<TileGroup type="multiple" defaultValue={["quiet"]} aria-label="What kind of day?">
  <Tile value="quiet">
    <TileMedia><img src="/quiet.jpg" alt="" /></TileMedia>
    <TileLabel>Quiet</TileLabel>
    <TileDescription>Gardens, reading rooms, slow walks</TileDescription>
  </Tile>
  <Tile value="lively">
    <TileMedia><img src="/lively.jpg" alt="" /></TileMedia>
    <TileLabel>Lively</TileLabel>
  </Tile>
</TileGroup>
```

### time-picker

A time field made of an hour and a minute that are each stepped with the arrow keys or typed, with an AM/PM part where the locale uses a 12-hour clock. The value is a 24-hour "HH:mm" string.

Use it: Any time of the person's own choosing: an opening hour, a reminder, an arrival. When the times on offer are a fixed list use slot-picker. Never the browser's native time input. Name it with `aria-label` or `aria-labelledby`.

```tsx
<p id="opens-label">Opens at</p>
<TimePicker aria-labelledby="opens-label" defaultValue="09:30" minuteStep={5} name="opens" locale="en-GB" />

// Controlled, limited, 12-hour whatever the locale, with translated names
<TimePicker
  value={time}
  onValueChange={setTime}
  min="08:00"
  max="18:00"
  hourCycle={12}
  aria-label="Pick-up time"
  labels={{ hour: "Hour", minute: "Minute", period: "Morning or afternoon", empty: "Not set" }}
/>
```

### timeline

An ordered list of numbered rows joined by a line: each with an optional time, a title and content, and a state (done, current, upcoming).

Use it: Things that happen in an order: the parts of a day, the stages of an order or a delivery, a history of changes, the steps of a plan. The number and the state are read out with each row. For the steps of a form the person is filling in use steps; for rows people reorder use sortable-list; for unordered items use a plain list.

```tsx
<Timeline aria-label="Saturday">
  <TimelineItem state="done">
    <TimelineTime dateTime="2026-03-14T09:30">09:30</TimelineTime>
    <TimelineTitle>Market walk</TimelineTitle>
    <TimelineContent>Meet at the north gate.</TimelineContent>
  </TimelineItem>
  <TimelineItem state="current">
    <TimelineTime dateTime="2026-03-14T12:30">12:30</TimelineTime>
    <TimelineTitle>Lunch</TimelineTitle>
  </TimelineItem>
  <TimelineItem>
    <TimelineTitle>Free afternoon</TimelineTitle>
  </TimelineItem>
</Timeline>
```

### toaster

The place where toasts appear: sonner's Toaster drawn with the theme's tokens, and its `toast` function.

Use it: Short confirmations and errors that need no decision ("Saved", "Could not connect"). Render one Toaster in the root layout, then call `toast` from anywhere on the client. For something that must be answered use dialog; for a message that belongs to a field or a section, show it there.

```tsx
// app/layout.tsx
<body>
  {children}
  <Toaster />
</body>

// any client component
<Button onClick={() => toast.success("Saved", { description: "Your changes are live." })}>Save</Button>
```

### toggle-group

A joined row of toggles where one (type="single") or several (type="multiple") are on.

Use it: A compact choice between a few short options or icons: alignment, a view switcher, text styles. For options with longer labels use radio-group (one) or checkboxes (several); for switching panels use tabs.

```tsx
<ToggleGroup type="single" defaultValue="grid" aria-label="View" variant="outline">
  <ToggleGroupItem value="grid">Grid</ToggleGroupItem>
  <ToggleGroupItem value="list">List</ToggleGroupItem>
</ToggleGroup>
<ToggleGroup type="multiple" aria-label="Text style" size="sm">
  <ToggleGroupItem value="italic" aria-label="Italic"><Italic strokeWidth={1.5} /></ToggleGroupItem>
  <ToggleGroupItem value="underline" aria-label="Underline"><Underline strokeWidth={1.5} /></ToggleGroupItem>
</ToggleGroup>
```

### toggle

A button that stays pressed: on or off.

Use it: A toolbar state such as bold, mute or pin. For a setting use switch; for several toggles that belong together, or a pick-one row, use toggle-group.

```tsx
<Toggle aria-label="Italic"><Italic strokeWidth={1.5} /></Toggle>
<Toggle variant="outline" size="sm" defaultPressed>Pinned</Toggle>
```

### tooltip

A few words that appear beside a control on hover or keyboard focus.

Use it: Naming an icon-only button or adding a short hint. It does not open on touch, so never put anything needed there: the control keeps its own `aria-label`. For content people interact with use popover. Put one TooltipProvider around the app (root layout); every Tooltip must be inside one.

```tsx
<TooltipProvider>
  <Tooltip>
    <TooltipTrigger asChild>
      <Button variant="ghost" size="icon" aria-label="Copy link"><Link2 /></Button>
    </TooltipTrigger>
    <TooltipContent>Copy link</TooltipContent>
  </Tooltip>
</TooltipProvider>
```

### undo-line

A line that stays where something was just done, says what it was, and offers to undo it.

Use it: After an action that can be taken back, inside the place it happened: a row removed from a plan, a message archived, a change applied by an assistant. It stays until it is dismissed or the next action replaces it, so it is not missed the way a toast is by someone using a screen reader, a magnifier or a slow hand. For news that needs no answer and is unrelated to one place use toaster; for a decision before the action use dialog.

```tsx
{removed ? (
  <UndoLine>
    <UndoLineMessage>Lunch was removed from Saturday.</UndoLineMessage>
    <UndoLineAction onClick={restore}>Undo</UndoLineAction>
    <UndoLineDismiss aria-label="Dismiss" onClick={() => setRemoved(null)} />
  </UndoLine>
) : null}
```

### video-player

The parts of a video player around a `<video>` element the project renders: a frame that keeps its shape, controls that step back while it plays, play, mute, volume, time, a scrubber, captions, speed, full screen, and words for loading and failure.

Use it: Any video a person controls: a clip on a page, a lesson, a recording. The project gives the element its sources (a file, or HLS attached to the element); the parts only drive it, so compose the ones the clip needs. Nothing plays by itself: for a silent, looping decoration use a plain `<video muted loop>` with its own pause control. For sound alone use audio-player; for a picture viewer use lightbox.

```tsx
<VideoPlayer aria-label="How the kiln is loaded" defaultCaptions>
  <VideoPlayerVideo src="/kiln.mp4" poster="/kiln.jpg">
    <track kind="captions" src="/kiln.en.vtt" srcLang="en" label="English" />
  </VideoPlayerVideo>
  <VideoPlayerLoading />
  <VideoPlayerError />
  <Captions />
  <VideoPlayerControls>
    <VideoPlayerScrubber />
    <VideoPlayerControlsRow>
      <VideoPlayerPlay />
      <VideoPlayerMute />
      <VideoPlayerVolume />
      <VideoPlayerTime />
      <VideoPlayerCaptionsButton className="ms-auto" />
      <VideoPlayerRate />
      <VideoPlayerFullscreen />
    </VideoPlayerControlsRow>
  </VideoPlayerControls>
</VideoPlayer>
```

### virtual-list

A long list or grid that renders only the rows in view: thousands of items of any height in a box that scrolls, or down a page that scrolls with the window, each still announced with its position in the whole list, with a way to go to an item and to come back to where the person was.

Use it: More items than the page should hold at once (a few hundred or more): a feed, a log, search results, a picture library. Rows may have any height: each is measured once it is drawn and the rest are estimated, and the view does not jump when a row above it turns out taller. Give the box a height and a name (`aria-label`); or, where the list is the page (a feed, results under a header), `scroll="window"` and no height: it then grows to its full length and the window scrolls it. For a short list render the rows plainly; for a conversation that grows at the bottom use thread; for pages of results use pagination. Written here on ResizeObserver instead of adding a virtualisation package: a headless one would bring the offsets but not the roles, the positions for screen readers, the kept focus or the restoration, which are most of this file.

```tsx
// Rows of any height
<VirtualList count={messages.length} estimateSize={72} getKey={(index) => messages[index].id} aria-label="Messages" className="h-96 rounded-surface border">
  {(index) => <article className="border-b p-3">{messages[index].text}</article>}
</VirtualList>

// A grid, as many columns as fit; the place is remembered for this tab
<VirtualGrid count={pictures.length} columns={{ minWidth: 160 }} gap={8} estimateSize={160} restoreKey="library" aria-label="Pictures" className="h-[32rem]">
  {(index) => <img src={pictures[index].src} alt={pictures[index].alt} className="aspect-square w-full rounded-control object-cover" />}
</VirtualGrid>

// The page scrolls, not a box: no height, and rows above and below the window are not rendered
<VirtualList scroll="window" count={results.length} estimateSize={96} getKey={(index) => results[index].id} aria-label="Results">
  {(index) => <ResultCard result={results[index]} />}
</VirtualList>

// Going to an item
const list = useRef<VirtualListHandle>(null);
<VirtualList handleRef={list} count={10000} aria-label="Lines">{(index) => <p className="p-2">Line {index + 1}</p>}</VirtualList>
<Button onClick={() => list.current?.scrollToIndex(4999, { align: "center" })}>Go to line 5,000</Button>
```

### wizard

The shell of a guided task done one step at a time inside a card: a title with "Step 2 of 5", a rail of the steps, the current step, and Back, Skip and a main button named after what the step does.

Use it: A task that is easier one question at a time and has a known order: a booking, a set-up, an application. It keeps where one is (controlled or not), moves focus to each new step's heading, and blocks the main button with a stated reason while a step is not answered. Where a server decides what comes next, control it: give `step`, and `onNext`, `onBack` and `onSkip` in place of the wizard's own moves, with `pending` while the answer is on its way; the step still slides in and its heading still takes focus when `step` changes. For a short form show all the fields at once (field); for the rail alone use steps; for unordered sections use tabs or accordion. What each step contains is yours: the wizard holds no answers.

```tsx
const [people, setPeople] = useState(0);
<Wizard
  steps={[
    { id: "dates", label: "Dates" },
    { id: "people", label: "People", canContinue: people > 0, blockedReason: "Say how many people are coming." },
    { id: "extras", label: "Extras", optional: true },
    { id: "review", label: "Review" },
  ]}
  defaultStep="dates"
  onComplete={book}
>
  <WizardHeader>Book a table</WizardHeader>
  <WizardRail />
  <WizardStep id="dates" title="Which day?">…</WizardStep>
  <WizardStep id="people" title="How many people?">…</WizardStep>
  <WizardStep id="extras" title="Anything to add?">…</WizardStep>
  <WizardStep id="review" title="Check and confirm">…</WizardStep>
  <WizardFooter>
    <WizardBack>Back</WizardBack>
    <WizardSkip>Skip</WizardSkip>
    <WizardNext>{step === "review" ? "Confirm" : "Continue"}</WizardNext>
  </WizardFooter>
</Wizard>

// Driven from outside: the server says which step is next, and the rail's states are the project's
<Wizard
  steps={flow.steps.map((item) => ({ id: item.id, label: item.label, optional: item.optional, state: item.skipped ? "skipped" : undefined }))}
  step={flow.current}
  pending={saving}
  onNext={(current) => submit(current.id)}
  onBack={(current) => goBackFrom(current.id)}
  onSkip={(current) => skip(current.id)}
>…</Wizard>
```

## Layout

### aspect

Holds its content at a fixed width-to-height ratio, so space is reserved before an image, video or canvas loads.

Use it: Media whose size is not known until it loads, or a tile that must keep its shape at any width. Make the child fill it (`size-full object-cover`). For plain CSS needs the `aspect-video` utility is enough.

```tsx
<Aspect ratio={16 / 9} className="rounded-surface border">
  <img src="/shots/hero.jpg" alt="The studio" className="size-full object-cover" />
</Aspect>
<Aspect ratio={1}><div className="size-full bg-muted" /></Aspect>
```

### bento-grid

A grid of flat cards of unequal sizes. One column on a phone, two on a tablet, then 2, 3, 4 or 6: decided by the grid's own width, so it works inside any container.

Use it: Showing several features, figures or pieces of media as one composed block. Cells take `span` and `rowSpan`; spans are clamped to the columns there are. For equal cards use grid; for a single surface use card.

```tsx
// Feature block: one wide lead cell, two small ones, a full-width strip.
<BentoGrid columns={3}>
  <BentoCell span={2} rowSpan={2}>
    <BentoCellHeader>
      <BentoCellTitle>Themable from one place</BentoCellTitle>
      <BentoCellDescription>Light or dark, square to round, any highlight colour.</BentoCellDescription>
    </BentoCellHeader>
    <BentoCellMedia><img src="/shots/theme.png" alt="" /></BentoCellMedia>
  </BentoCell>
  <BentoCell><BentoCellHeader><BentoCellTitle>Accessible</BentoCellTitle></BentoCellHeader></BentoCell>
  <BentoCell><BentoCellHeader><BentoCellTitle>Fast</BentoCellTitle></BentoCellHeader></BentoCell>
  <BentoCell span="full"><BentoCellHeader><BentoCellTitle>Yours to edit</BentoCellTitle></BentoCellHeader></BentoCell>
</BentoGrid>

// Dashboard: four figures on top, a wide chart beside a tall list.
<BentoGrid columns={4} rowHeight="8rem">
  <BentoCell><Stat label="Revenue" value="€48k" className="border-0" /></BentoCell>
  <BentoCell><Stat label="Orders" value="1,204" className="border-0" /></BentoCell>
  <BentoCell><Stat label="Visitors" value="18.2k" className="border-0" /></BentoCell>
  <BentoCell><Stat label="Refunds" value="12" className="border-0" /></BentoCell>
  <BentoCell span={3} rowSpan={3}>…chart…</BentoCell>
  <BentoCell rowSpan={3}>…recent activity…</BentoCell>
</BentoGrid>

// Link mosaic: six columns, mixed sizes, gaps back-filled, every cell a link.
<BentoGrid columns={6} dense>
  <BentoCell span={4} rowSpan={2} interactive asChild><a href="/work/atlas">…</a></BentoCell>
  <BentoCell span={2} interactive asChild><a href="/work/north">…</a></BentoCell>
  <BentoCell span={2} interactive asChild><a href="/work/field">…</a></BentoCell>
  <BentoCell span={3} interactive asChild><a href="/work/tide">…</a></BentoCell>
  <BentoCell span={3} interactive asChild><a href="/work/loom">…</a></BentoCell>
</BentoGrid>
```

### container

Centres content at the page width with the page gutter on both sides. Four sizes: narrow, page, wide, full.

Use it: Around the content of every page band so edges line up down the page. "narrow" for reading text, "wide" for galleries and dashboards, "full" to keep only the gutter. Section already wraps its children in one.

```tsx
<Container>
  <h1>Pricing</h1>
</Container>
<Container size="narrow" asChild>
  <article>Long-form text…</article>
</Container>
```

### grid

A responsive grid of equal columns that fits as many as the width allows, from a minimum column width. No breakpoints.

Use it: A set of like items: cards, logos, stats, thumbnails. It reflows inside any width, including a sidebar. For tiles of different sizes use bento-grid; for two fixed columns use split.

```tsx
<Grid min="16rem" gap="md">
  <Card>…</Card>
  <Card>…</Card>
  <Card>…</Card>
</Grid>
<Grid min="9rem" gap="sm" fit="fill">{logos}</Grid>
```

### map-frame

The frame around a map, not a map: it holds the map's size, shows a still until the person asks for the map, keeps a text list beside it, and takes the map to full screen and back. The map engine is yours.

Use it: Any page that shows a map from any engine (MapLibre, Leaflet, a hosted maps script). It gives the map what an engine does not: no request to a third party before the person presses the button (put the line about that in MapFrameNotice), no layout shift, the same information as a list (MapFrameList) so that the map is never the only way to it, a way to skip past the map with the keyboard, and full screen that behaves as a modal. For a still picture of a place with no interaction use an image in aspect.

```tsx
<MapFrame aria-label="Map of the three stops">
  <MapFrameStage className="aspect-video">
    <MapFramePlaceholder>
      <MapFrameActivate>Show the map</MapFrameActivate>
      <MapFrameNotice>The map is loaded from Example Maps, which will see your address.</MapFrameNotice>
    </MapFramePlaceholder>
    <MapFrameCanvas><MyMapEngine stops={stops} /></MapFrameCanvas>
    <MapFrameToolbar>
      <MapFrameFullscreen />
    </MapFrameToolbar>
  </MapFrameStage>
  <MapFrameList>
    <ol>{stops.map((stop) => <li key={stop.id}>{stop.name}, {stop.address}</li>)}</ol>
  </MapFrameList>
</MapFrame>
```

### marquee

A row that scrolls sideways without end. It pauses on hover and on keyboard focus, and under reduced motion it is an ordinary wrapped row.

Use it: A strip of logos, short quotes or tags where no single item must be read. Not for content the reader needs: everything is also in the markup once, but it moves. For a few items that fit, use stack or grid.

```tsx
<Marquee aria-label="Clients" speed="slow">
  <img src="/logos/atlas.svg" alt="Atlas" className="h-8 w-auto" />
  <img src="/logos/north.svg" alt="North" className="h-8 w-auto" />
  <img src="/logos/field.svg" alt="Field" className="h-8 w-auto" />
</Marquee>
<Marquee direction="right" speed={25} gap="1rem" fade={false}>
  <Badge variant="outline">Design</Badge>
  <Badge variant="outline">Build</Badge>
  <Badge variant="outline">Launch</Badge>
</Marquee>
```

### section

A band of a page with consistent vertical rhythm, an optional eyebrow, title and description, and three tones: default, muted, inverse.

Use it: Every top-level block of a marketing or content page. "inverse" makes a dark band on a light page and re-themes everything inside it. Inside an app screen use stack and card instead.

```tsx
<Section eyebrow="Features" title="Everything in one place" description="Built on the same tokens.">
  <BentoGrid>…</BentoGrid>
</Section>
<Section tone="inverse" align="center" title="Ready to start?">
  <Button>Get in touch</Button>
</Section>
<Section tone="muted" spacing="sm" container="narrow">Plain content, no header.</Section>
```

### split

Two columns, usually media beside text, that stack into one on a narrow width. A ratio between the columns and a reverse option.

Use it: A feature row, a hero with an image, a form beside its explanation. Give it exactly two children. Alternate `reverse` down a page for a zigzag. For more than two columns use grid.

```tsx
<Split ratio="3:2">
  <SplitMedia><img src="/shots/dashboard.png" alt="The dashboard" /></SplitMedia>
  <SplitContent>
    <h2 className="text-3xl font-medium">See everything at once</h2>
    <p className="text-muted-foreground">One screen for the whole week.</p>
  </SplitContent>
</Split>
<Split reverse align="start" gap="lg">
  <SplitMedia>…</SplitMedia>
  <SplitContent>…</SplitContent>
</Split>
```

### stack

A flex row or column with a gap from a fixed scale, and props for alignment, distribution and wrapping.

Use it: Spacing a run of siblings evenly: form fields, a button row, a header with actions. For columns that reflow by width use grid; for unequal tiles use bento-grid.

```tsx
<Stack gap="lg">
  <h2>Title</h2>
  <p>Body</p>
</Stack>
<Stack direction="horizontal" gap="sm" align="center" justify="between" wrap>
  <span>Plan</span>
  <Button size="sm">Change</Button>
</Stack>
<Stack asChild gap="xs"><ul><li>One</li><li>Two</li></ul></Stack>
```

## Motion and transitions

### explainer

Turns an explainer spec (plain JSON: scenes of a title, any chart, a map, a 3D model, a then-and-now comparison, a quote or a caption) into a film on film-stage: playable, scrubbable, with captions, narration in step, a provenance label on every scene that says how it was made, and frames drawn on request for export.

Use it: An assistant or a project describes a short explanatory film as data and wants it played: a story with numbers, a report as a film, a change on a map. Validate the spec with lib/explainer-spec first; a spec with faults shows them in words instead of a film. For a film drawn by hand use film-stage; for a video file use video-player.

```tsx
<Explainer spec={spec} />

// Arranged by the project, and exported frame by frame by scripts/export-film.ts
<Explainer spec={spec} deterministic exportName="main">
  <FilmStageFrame aspect={16 / 9}>
    <ExplainerProvenance />
    <ExplainerCaptions />
  </FilmStageFrame>
</Explainer>
```

### film-stage

A stage for a sequence of timed scenes with a transport: it owns the clock and the chrome (play, time bar, speed, sound), mounts the scene for the current moment, cuts or crossfades between scenes, and can draw any moment on request for export.

Use it: Content the project draws itself from a time: an animated explainer, a story in scenes, a slideshow with narration, a film assembled from markup, SVG or canvas. Each scene gets its own local time and draws from it, so any frame can be drawn again exactly. The stage is the clock other things follow: scrubber, scene-strip, captions and hotspots work inside it as they do inside video-player, and any number of sounds (a clip for each narrated line, a bed under them) are kept in step, each from its own start for its own length. For a video or sound file use video-player or audio-player; for motion tied to scrolling use scroll-scene; for a set of pictures a person pages through use carousel.

```tsx
const scenes = [
  { id: "title", duration: 4, label: "Title", children: <h2 className="p-8 text-3xl">How a pot is thrown</h2> },
  { id: "wheel", duration: 6, label: "On the wheel", transition: "crossfade" as const, render: ({ progress }) => <Wheel turn={progress} /> },
];
<FilmStage scenes={scenes} aria-label="How a pot is thrown">
  <FilmStageFrame aspect={16 / 9}>
    <Captions cues={cues} lang="en" />
  </FilmStageFrame>
  <FilmStageAudio src="/narration.mp3" />
  <FilmStageControls>
    <FilmStageScrubber />
    <FilmStageControlsRow>
      <FilmStagePreviousScene />
      <FilmStagePlay />
      <FilmStageNextScene />
      <FilmStageMute />
      <FilmStageTime />
      <FilmStageRate className="ms-auto" />
    </FilmStageControlsRow>
  </FilmStageControls>
  <FilmStageSceneStrip />
</FilmStage>

// One clip for each narrated line and a bed under them; each follows the clock, the speed, a seek and the mute
<FilmStage scenes={scenes} loop onSceneChange={(scene) => track(scene.id)} aria-label="How a pot is thrown">
  <FilmStageFrame />
  <FilmStageAudio src="/bed.mp3" volume={0.3} />
  {lines.map((line) => <FilmStageAudio key={line.id} src={line.src} start={line.start} duration={line.length} />)}
</FilmStage>

// Export: a headless browser draws each frame, with no timer running on the page
<FilmStage scenes={scenes} deterministic exportName="main" aria-label="How a pot is thrown">…</FilmStage>
// in the page, from the exporter: await window.__filmStage.main.renderAt(frame / 30), then take the picture
```

### layout-transition

A shared element that animates from one place to another: render Morph with the same layoutId in two places and it travels between them.

Use it: A tabs or navigation indicator that slides to the active item, a card that grows into its detail view, a selection highlight. Both places must be in the same React tree. Between pages use view-transition; for content that only appears and disappears use presence.

```tsx
const [active, setActive] = useState("overview");
<MorphGroup id="section-tabs">
  <div className="flex gap-1">
    {["overview", "pricing", "docs"].map((tab) => (
      <button key={tab} onClick={() => setActive(tab)} className="relative h-control rounded-control px-4 text-sm">
        {active === tab ? <Morph layoutId="indicator" className="absolute inset-0 rounded-control bg-accent" /> : null}
        <span className="relative capitalize">{tab}</span>
      </button>
    ))}
  </div>
</MorphGroup>
```

### magnetic

A wrapper whose child is gently pulled toward the pointer while it is hovered, and springs back when the pointer leaves.

Use it: The one main call to action on a marketing page, or an icon button that should feel alive. Not for every button, not inside dense interfaces, and it does nothing on touch screens.

```tsx
<Magnetic>
  <Button size="lg">Start a project</Button>
</Magnetic>
<Magnetic strength={0.5}>
  <Button variant="outline" size="icon" aria-label="Play"><Play /></Button>
</Magnetic>
```

### number-ticker

A number that counts up to its value when it scrolls into view, formatted with Intl.NumberFormat.

Use it: A headline statistic: customers, revenue, a percentage. Not for values that update live (render those directly), and not for more than a few on one screen.

```tsx
<NumberTicker value={12480} />
<NumberTicker value={0.9997} options={{ style: "percent", maximumFractionDigits: 2 }} />
<NumberTicker value={48000} locale="de-DE" options={{ style: "currency", currency: "EUR", maximumFractionDigits: 0 }} />
```

### page-transition

Wraps page content and plays a short enter (a fade and a small rise) each time the route changes.

Use it: The content area of an app or site, once, in the layout. The first page load is not animated. Where the browser supports it and elements should morph between pages, use view-transition instead; do not use both.

```tsx
// app/template.tsx (Next.js). A template is re-created on navigation; the pathname is the key.
"use client";
import { usePathname } from "next/navigation";
import type { ReactNode } from "react";
import { PageTransition } from "@/components/motion/page-transition";

export default function Template({ children }: { children: ReactNode }) {
  return <PageTransition routeKey={usePathname()}>{children}</PageTransition>;
}
```

### parallax

A clipped frame whose layer moves at a different speed from the page as it scrolls past.

Use it: A background image or a decorative layer behind a section. The frame needs a height of its own (an aspect ratio or a fixed height). Not for text that must be read while it moves; for a pinned, scroll-told sequence use scroll-scene.

```tsx
<Parallax speed={0.3} className="aspect-video rounded-surface">
  <img src="/landscape.jpg" alt="" className="size-full object-cover" />
</Parallax>
```

### presence

Animates its children in when they are shown and out before they are removed.

Use it: Conditional UI that is not a Radix primitive: an inline notice, a revealed panel, a step that swaps. Radix dialogs, popovers and menus already animate with their own classes; for content entering on scroll use reveal.

```tsx
const [open, setOpen] = useState(false);
<Button onClick={() => setOpen((value) => !value)}>Toggle</Button>
<Presence show={open} preset="slide-up" className="mt-4 rounded-surface border p-4">
  Saved. Your changes are live.
</Presence>
```

### reveal

Fades and moves its content into place when it scrolls into view.

Use it: A section, card or image that should arrive as the page is read. For a list revealed one after another use stagger; for a heading use text-reveal; for conditional UI that mounts and unmounts use presence.

```tsx
<Reveal>
  <h2 className="text-2xl font-medium">Built to be owned</h2>
</Reveal>
<Reveal direction="start" distance={40} delay={0.1} once={false}>
  <img src="/studio.jpg" alt="The studio" className="rounded-surface" />
</Reveal>
```

### scroll-progress

A thin bar fixed to the top of the viewport that fills as the page, or one element, is scrolled through.

Use it: Long reading pages: an article, documentation, a case study. Pass `target` to follow the article rather than the whole page. Not a loading indicator (use a progress control for that).

```tsx
<ScrollProgress />

const article = useRef<HTMLElement>(null);
<ScrollProgress target={article} className="h-1" />
<article ref={article}>…</article>
```

### scroll-scene

A tall section with a pinned viewport whose children are driven by scroll progress from 0 to 1, for scroll-told sequences.

Use it: A product story told as the visitor scrolls: steps that replace each other, a device that turns, a diagram that builds. Use sparingly, one or two per page. For a simple entrance use reveal; for a drifting background use parallax.

```tsx
<ScrollScene length={3}>
  <ScrollSceneStep from={0} to={0.33} className="grid place-items-center p-6">
    <h2 className="text-3xl font-medium">Design</h2>
  </ScrollSceneStep>
  <ScrollSceneStep from={0.33} to={0.66} className="grid place-items-center p-6">
    <h2 className="text-3xl font-medium">Build</h2>
  </ScrollSceneStep>
  <ScrollSceneStep from={0.66} to={1} className="grid place-items-center p-6">
    <h2 className="text-3xl font-medium">Launch</h2>
  </ScrollSceneStep>
</ScrollScene>

<ScrollScene length={2}>
  {(progress, active) => <Dial progress={progress} still={!active} />}
</ScrollScene>

function Dial({ progress, still }: { progress: MotionValue<number>; still: boolean }) {
  const rotate = useTransform(progress, [0, 1], [0, 180]);
  return <motion.div className="size-40 border" style={{ rotate: still ? 0 : rotate }} />;
}
```

### spotlight

A surface on which a soft light in the highlight colour follows the pointer.

Use it: A hero panel, a feature card or a call-to-action band that should respond to the pointer. Give it a border and a background like any surface. Decoration only: it does nothing on touch screens, so never rely on it to show something.

```tsx
<Spotlight className="rounded-surface border bg-card p-8">
  <h3 className="text-xl font-medium">Made to be changed</h3>
  <p className="text-muted-foreground">Every component is yours to edit.</p>
</Spotlight>
<Spotlight size={640} className="rounded-surface border p-12">…</Spotlight>
```

### stagger

A container whose items fade and move into place one after another when it scrolls into view.

Use it: A grid of cards, a feature list, a row of logos. For one block use reveal; for the words of a heading use text-reveal.

```tsx
<Stagger className="grid gap-4 sm:grid-cols-3" interval={0.08}>
  <StaggerItem><Card>Design</Card></StaggerItem>
  <StaggerItem><Card>Build</Card></StaggerItem>
  <StaggerItem><Card>Launch</Card></StaggerItem>
</Stagger>
```

### text-reveal

Reveals a heading word by word, or line by line, when it scrolls into view.

Use it: A headline or a short statement. Not for paragraphs of body text (use reveal on the block), and not for text that changes while it is shown.

```tsx
<TextReveal as="h1" className="text-4xl font-medium" playOnLoad>
  Websites, apps and systems that last
</TextReveal>
<TextReveal as="p" by="line" interval={0.12} className="max-w-prose text-xl">
  We design the brand, build the product and stay to run it.
</TextReveal>
```

### tilt

A wrapper that tilts its content in 3D toward the pointer on hover and springs back, with an optional glare.

Use it: A featured card, a product shot, a pricing plan worth lifting off the page. One or a few per view; not for forms or anything read at length, and it does nothing on touch screens.

```tsx
<Tilt max={8} glare className="max-w-sm">
  <Card>
    <CardHeader>
      <CardTitle>Studio plan</CardTitle>
      <CardDescription>Everything, for one team</CardDescription>
    </CardHeader>
  </Card>
</Tilt>
```

### view-transition

View transitions two ways: wrappers over React's own <ViewTransition> (a shared element that morphs between two places, a boundary that cross-fades what changes inside it), and helpers for the browser's API (run an update as a transition, name an element, a link that navigates inside a transition).

Use it: Moving between pages or between two states of a view, where an element in the old view should become one in the new. Use the React wrappers (SharedElement, TransitionBoundary) when the change is a React transition: a state update inside startTransition, a Suspense boundary revealing, a navigation by a router that uses transitions (Next.js). React then starts the browser's transition itself. Use the browser helpers (startViewTransition, ViewTransitionName, TransitionLink) when nothing in the tree uses React's component: a synchronous update, a router that does not use transitions, an element that stays mounted while the view around it changes. Do not mix the two for one update: React's documentation says not to call document.startViewTransition yourself around an update it is already animating. Both degrade to an instant change where the API is missing, and the theme switches them off under reduced motion. For a shared element that must be interrupted mid-way use layout-transition; for a simple enter on route change use page-transition.

```tsx
// React's way: the same name in two places; the update runs in a transition.
const [open, setOpen] = useState(false);
{open ? (
  <SharedElement name="atlas-cover"><img src="/atlas.jpg" alt="Atlas" className="w-full" /></SharedElement>
) : (
  <button onClick={() => startTransition(() => setOpen(true))}>
    <SharedElement name="atlas-cover"><img src="/atlas.jpg" alt="Atlas" className="size-24" /></SharedElement>
  </button>
)}

// The browser's way. A link that navigates inside a view transition; in Next.js pass router.push:
<TransitionLink href="/work/atlas" navigate={router.push}>Atlas</TransitionLink>
// The same name on the list page and on the detail page: the image morphs from one to the other.
<ViewTransitionName name="work-atlas-cover" asChild>
  <img src="/atlas.jpg" alt="Atlas" />
</ViewTransitionName>
// A state change in place. flushSync (from react-dom) makes React apply it before the browser's snapshot.
<Button onClick={() => startViewTransition(() => flushSync(() => setLayout("grid")))}>Grid</Button>
```

## 3D

### floating-shapes

A few simple solids (icosahedron, torus, box, octahedron) floating and turning slowly, flat-shaded or wireframe, coloured from theme variables.

Use it: An abstract, geometric accent for a hero or a feature section. Use it inside scene. For a single soft object use orb; to show a real object use model-stage.

```tsx
<Scene aspect={16 / 9}>
  <FloatingShapes />
</Scene>

<Scene aspect={2}>
  <FloatingShapes
    shapes={[
      { kind: "torus", position: [-1.5, 0, 0], color: "--highlight" },
      { kind: "box", position: [1.5, 0.4, -1], size: 0.8, color: "--foreground", wireframe: true },
    ]}
  />
</Scene>
```

### globe

A dotted globe that turns slowly and can be dragged to spin, with optional highlighted markers by latitude and longitude.

Use it: Showing reach or places at a glance: offices, regions, where requests come from. Use it inside scene. For exact values per place use a table or bar-chart; the globe is not a chart.

```tsx
<Scene aspect={1} className="max-w-lg" label="A globe with markers on Amsterdam, Kochi and San Francisco">
  <Globe
    markers={[
      { lat: 52.37, lon: 4.9 },
      { lat: 9.93, lon: 76.27 },
      { lat: 37.77, lon: -122.42 },
    ]}
  />
</Scene>
```

### model-stage

A turntable for any mesh or group: centres and fits it, turns it slowly, and lets the pointer orbit it within limits.

Use it: Showing one object: a product, a loaded model, a shape of your own. Use it inside scene. For decoration without a subject use orb or floating-shapes.

```tsx
<Scene aspect={4 / 3} label="A turning torus knot">
  <ModelStage>
    <mesh>
      <torusKnotGeometry args={[1, 0.32, 128, 16]} />
      <meshStandardMaterial flatShading />
    </mesh>
  </ModelStage>
</Scene>
```

### model-viewer

Shows one 3D model that a person can turn, zoom and reset: a glTF or GLB file, or Gaussian splats (.spz, .ply, .splat, .ksplat, .sog), with a poster and progress while it loads and a still fallback where 3D cannot run.

Use it: A file to look at from every side: an object, a product, a scanned place. It is a whole viewer, not a part of scene: for your own meshes inside a react-three-fiber canvas use scene with model-stage. Nothing heavy is in this file: three.js is fetched when the viewer comes near the screen, its glTF loader only for glTF, and Spark (`@sparkjsdev/spark`, installed with this item) only when the file is splats. glTF that carries splats in an extension is not read (Spark has no glTF loader); Draco, Meshopt and KTX2 compression need their decoders set in `configureLoader`. Plain wheel and vertical swipes scroll the page: zoom is pinch, Ctrl with the wheel, the keys or the buttons. To compare two models, give two viewers the same `view` and `bounds` inside compare-slider, with `children={null}` and buttons of your own that change the shared view.

```tsx
<ModelViewer src="/models/vase.glb" alt="A clay vase with a painted belt" poster="/models/vase.jpg" />

// Splats, turning by itself (never under reduced motion), with a hand-off to AR on phones
<ModelViewer
  src="/models/courtyard.spz"
  alt="The courtyard, scanned in 2026"
  autoRotate
  rotation={[180, 0, 0]}
  ar={{ usdz: "/models/courtyard.usdz", glb: "https://example.com/models/courtyard.glb" }}
/>

// Two viewers, one camera
const [view, setView] = useState<ModelView>({ azimuth: 0, polar: 15, zoom: 1 });
const frame = { center: [0, 4, 0], radius: 9 } as const; // one sphere for both, so they keep their sizes and line up
<ModelViewer src="/models/then.glb" alt="As built" view={view} onViewChange={setView} bounds={frame} />
<ModelViewer src="/models/now.glb" alt="Today" view={view} onViewChange={setView} bounds={frame} />
```

### orb

A softly morphing sphere in the highlight colour, lit at its rim so it reads on light and dark grounds, leaning gently toward the pointer.

Use it: A calm focal object for a hero or an empty state. Use it inside scene. For many small elements use particle-field; for a product or object of your own use model-stage.

```tsx
<Scene aspect={1} className="max-w-md">
  <Orb />
</Scene>

<Scene aspect={16 / 9}>
  <Orb color="--chart-2" speed={0.6} distortion={0.5} detail={32} />
</Scene>
```

### particle-field

A field of small round points drifting slowly, with depth that shifts as the pointer moves.

Use it: A quiet moving ground behind a hero or a section. Use it inside scene and keep text on top readable. For one focal object use orb; for data use the viz components, never particles.

```tsx
<Scene className="absolute inset-0">
  <ParticleField />
</Scene>

<Scene aspect={2}>
  <ParticleField count={400} color="--foreground" size={0.03} spread={10} />
</Scene>
```

### scene

The wrapper every 3D component is used inside: a transparent WebGL canvas that mounts late, pauses off screen and falls back to a static block.

Use it: Around orb, particle-field, floating-shapes, globe, model-stage or your own react-three-fiber content. Give it a size through the parent or `aspect`. For a decorative background that needs no 3D, use a plain token-coloured block.

```tsx
<Scene aspect={16 / 9} label="A slowly morphing sphere">
  <Orb />
</Scene>

<div className="h-80">
  <Scene fallback={<img src="/globe.png" alt="" className="size-full object-contain" />}>
    <Globe markers={[{ lat: 52.37, lon: 4.9 }]} />
  </Scene>
</div>
```

## Visualisation

### area-chart

A line chart with the space under each line filled flat at low opacity, optionally stacked so the series add up to a total.

Use it: One series over time whose volume matters, or a few series that add up to a whole (`stacked`). To compare series that cross each other use line-chart: overlapping fills hide one another.

```tsx
<AreaChart
  label="Storage used per month, by kind"
  data={[
    { month: new Date("2026-01-01"), images: 12, video: 30 },
    { month: new Date("2026-02-01"), images: 18, video: 42 },
    { month: new Date("2026-03-01"), images: 22, video: 61 },
  ]}
  x="month"
  series={[
    { key: "images", label: "Images" },
    { key: "video", label: "Video" },
  ]}
  stacked
/>
```

### bar-chart

A bar chart, vertical or horizontal, grouped or stacked, always measured from zero, with a tooltip on hover and arrow-key reading.

Use it: Comparing amounts across categories. Use `orientation="horizontal"` for long names or a ranking, `stacked` when the series add up to a total, `normalize` to compare each category's split as shares of 100 %. For change over many points in time use line-chart; for a single number use a stat, not one bar.

```tsx
<BarChart
  label="Orders by channel per quarter"
  data={[
    { quarter: "Q1", web: 320, app: 210 },
    { quarter: "Q2", web: 410, app: 290 },
    { quarter: "Q3", web: 380, app: 350 },
  ]}
  x="quarter"
  series={[
    { key: "web", label: "Web" },
    { key: "app", label: "App" },
  ]}
  showValues
/>
```

### box-plot

The spread of a measure in each of several groups side by side: a box from the first to the third quartile, the median across it, whiskers to the furthest values within 1.5 boxes, and the values beyond them as points; or, as a violin, the shape of each spread.

Use it: Comparing distributions across groups: which is higher, which is wider, which has outliers. For one group's full shape use histogram; for a few exact numbers per group use bar-chart or dot-plot.

```tsx
<BoxPlot
  label="Response time by region"
  data={[
    { region: "North", ms: 120 }, { region: "North", ms: 140 }, { region: "North", ms: 135 }, { region: "North", ms: 310 },
    { region: "South", ms: 90 }, { region: "South", ms: 110 }, { region: "South", ms: 105 }, { region: "South", ms: 98 },
  ]}
  group="region"
  value="ms"
  valueLabel="Milliseconds"
/>
```

### bullet-chart

One measure against its target and its bands (poor, fair, good) in a single slim row: the value as a bar, the target as a tick, the bands as steps of grey behind them. Several rows stack, each on its own scale.

Use it: Showing how a few measures stand against their goals in little space: a dashboard of targets, a scorecard. For one value against a limit with nothing else use radial-progress or progress; to compare many values with each other use bar-chart.

```tsx
<BulletChart
  label="Quarter targets"
  items={[
    { label: "Revenue", value: 270, target: 250, ranges: [150, 225, 300] },
    { label: "New customers", value: 1400, target: 1600, ranges: [1000, 1500, 2000] },
  ]}
/>
```

### calendar-heatmap

A value per day laid out as a calendar, a column for each week and a row for each weekday, coloured on one hue from faint to strong, with month and weekday names and arrow keys that move by day and by week.

Use it: Showing a daily measure over months: activity, sales per day, rainfall, where the pattern by weekday and season matters. For a few weeks with exact values use bar-chart; for a trend use line-chart; to pick a day use calendar.

```tsx
<CalendarHeatmap
  label="Workouts per day"
  data={[{ day: "2026-01-05", count: 1 }, { day: "2026-01-06", count: 2 }, { day: "2026-01-09", count: 1 }]}
  day="day"
  value="count"
  from="2026-01-01"
  to="2026-03-31"
/>
```

### candlestick-chart

Opening, highest, lowest and closing values per period (a price, a reading): a thin line from low to high, a body from open to close, filled when it closed lower and hollow when it closed higher, so the direction is never colour alone.

Use it: Showing the range and the direction of a value within each period: prices by day, temperatures by day with their extremes. For the close alone use line-chart; for spread across many observations use box-plot.

```tsx
<CandlestickChart
  label="Price by day"
  data={[
    { day: new Date("2026-03-02"), open: 10, high: 12, low: 9.5, close: 11.4 },
    { day: new Date("2026-03-03"), open: 11.4, high: 11.8, low: 10.1, close: 10.3 },
    { day: new Date("2026-03-04"), open: 10.3, high: 11, low: 10, close: 10.9 },
  ]}
  x="day"
/>
```

### chart-brush

A small overview of a whole series with a window over it whose two handles are dragged or moved by arrow keys to choose the stretch another chart shows: the range is two row indexes, so it fits any chart.

Use it: Letting people zoom a long time series to a part of it: a year of daily values shown a month at a time. Give the chart above only the rows between the two indexes. For a fixed set of periods use segmented-control or tabs; for choosing dates use date-picker.

```tsx
const [range, setRange] = useState<[number, number]>([0, 29]);
<LineChart label="Visits" data={days.slice(range[0], range[1] + 1)} x="day" series={[{ key: "visits", label: "Visits" }]} />
<ChartBrush data={days} x="day" y="visits" value={range} onValueChange={setRange} labels={{ start: "From", end: "To" }} />
```

### chart

The shared parts every chart is built from: a container that measures itself and carries the text alternative, an SVG root, a tooltip, a legend, series styles, and axis and format helpers.

Use it: Building a chart of your own that should match the others. For the common forms use line-chart, area-chart, bar-chart, donut-chart, sparkline, heatmap or radial-progress directly.

```tsx
<ChartContainer aspect={2} table={{ caption: "Signups", columns: ["Day", "Signups"], rows: [["Mon", 4], ["Tue", 9]] }}>
  {({ width, height }) => (
    <ChartSvg label="Signups by day" width={width} height={height}>
      <rect x={0} y={height - 40} width={width / 3} height={40} className={chartSeries(0).fill} />
      <rect x={width / 2} y={height - 90} width={width / 3} height={90} className={chartSeries(0).fill} />
    </ChartSvg>
  )}
</ChartContainer>
<ChartLegend items={[{ label: "Signups", index: 0 }]} mark="rect" />
```

### chord-diagram

Flows between the members of one group, both ways, around a circle: each member an arc sized by all it sends, each ribbon joining two members with ends as wide as what goes each way, lit with its member on hover or focus.

Use it: Showing exchanges within a set where both directions matter: moves between regions, trade between countries, messages between teams. Keep it to about a dozen members. For flows in one direction through stages use sankey-chart; for links without amounts use network-graph.

```tsx
<ChordDiagram
  label="Moves between neighbourhoods"
  names={["North", "South", "East"]}
  matrix={[
    [0, 120, 40],
    [80, 0, 60],
    [30, 90, 0],
  ]}
/>
```

### choropleth

A geo-map layer that colours each region by a number, on one hue from faint to strong, on two hues either side of a midpoint, or in classes with stated edges; with a legend that says each step's range in words and a table of every region's value.

Use it: Showing a rate or a share that varies by region: turnout by district, rainfall by county. Use rates, not raw counts (large regions look important whatever their count); for counts use geo-markers bubbles. Goes inside geo-map.

```tsx
const scale = choroplethScale(regions.features.map((f) => f.properties.rate), { thresholds: [10, 20, 30] });
<GeoMap label="Rate by region" fit={regions}>
  <Choropleth label="Rate by region" data={regions} value={(f) => f.properties?.rate} name={(f) => f.properties?.name} scale={scale} />
</GeoMap>
<ChoroplethLegend title="Rate (%)" scale={scale} />
```

### circle-pack

A hierarchy as circles inside circles: each group an outline holding its parts, each part a circle whose area is its size, with zooming into a group by click or Enter and back out by the trail or Backspace.

Use it: Showing groups and their members when the grouping matters more than precise sizes: topics and their articles, teams and their projects. To compare sizes closely use treemap or bar-chart; for levels as rings use sunburst.

```tsx
<CirclePack
  label="Articles by topic"
  data={{
    name: "All articles",
    children: [
      { name: "Science", children: [{ name: "Space", value: 40 }, { name: "Biology", value: 25 }] },
      { name: "Arts", children: [{ name: "Film", value: 30 }, { name: "Music", value: 18 }] },
    ],
  }}
/>
```

### density-chart

Where many points crowd together, drawn as filled contour bands of one hue from faint to strong (like the lines of a height map), with the points optionally on top and each point reachable by arrow keys.

Use it: Two measures over hundreds or thousands of points, where a scatter-chart would be a blot: where the bulk lies, whether there are two clusters. For under a few hundred points use scatter-chart; for one measure's spread use histogram.

```tsx
<DensityChart
  label="Trip length against fare"
  data={[{ km: 2, fare: 8 }, { km: 3, fare: 10 }, { km: 2.5, fare: 9 }, { km: 12, fare: 31 }, { km: 11, fare: 29 }]}
  x="km"
  y="fare"
  xLabel="Distance (km)"
  yLabel="Fare"
  showPoints
/>
```

### donut-chart

A ring showing how one whole splits into at most five parts, with a label in the centre and each part's value and share in the legend.

Use it: Parts of a whole at a glance, when there are few parts and they differ clearly. To compare parts that are close in size, or more than five, use bar-chart with `orientation="horizontal"`; for one ratio against a limit use radial-progress.

```tsx
<DonutChart
  label="Traffic by source"
  data={[
    { source: "Search", visits: 5200 },
    { source: "Direct", visits: 3100 },
    { source: "Referral", visits: 1400 },
  ]}
  name="source"
  value="visits"
  centerLabel="Visits"
/>
```

### dot-plot

Values as dots along a shared axis, one row per category: plain dots for one or more series, a lollipop (a stick to the dot), a dumbbell (two values joined, for a before and after), or a beeswarm (every single value as its own dot, packed so none overlap).

Use it: Comparing values across categories with less ink than bars, especially when zero is not meaningful (dot, dumbbell), showing a change between two moments per category (dumbbell), or showing every observation in a few groups (beeswarm). For totals from zero use bar-chart; for a summary of spread use box-plot.

```tsx
<DotPlot
  label="Satisfaction before and after"
  data={[
    { team: "Support", before: 62, after: 78 },
    { team: "Sales", before: 70, after: 74 },
    { team: "Product", before: 55, after: 71 },
  ]}
  y="team"
  series={[{ key: "before", label: "Before" }, { key: "after", label: "After" }]}
  variant="dumbbell"
/>
```

### fan-chart

A forecast drawn honestly: what was observed as a solid line, then the median forecast with nested bands for its intervals (90 %, 50 % …) that widen as the forecast reaches further, with arrow-key reading of every point.

Use it: Showing a prediction or an estimate with its uncertainty: a forecast, a model's range, a confidence band around a trend. For a series with no uncertainty use line-chart; for the spread of measured values use box-plot.

```tsx
<FanChart
  label="Visitors, observed and forecast"
  data={[
    { week: 1, observed: 120 },
    { week: 2, observed: 132 },
    { week: 3, observed: 128, median: 128, low90: 128, high90: 128, low50: 128, high50: 128 },
    { week: 4, median: 136, low90: 118, high90: 152, low50: 128, high50: 143 },
    { week: 5, median: 141, low90: 110, high90: 170, low50: 126, high50: 155 },
  ]}
  x="week"
  observed="observed"
  median="median"
  intervals={[
    { low: "low90", high: "high90", label: "90% interval" },
    { low: "low50", high: "high50", label: "50% interval" },
  ]}
  forecastFrom={3}
  labels={{ observed: "Observed", median: "Forecast (median)", forecast: "Forecast" }}
/>
```

### funnel-chart

The steps of a process that people (or things) drop out of, as centred bars that narrow with the count, each with its count, its share of the first step and its share of the step before.

Use it: Showing where a sequence loses the most: sign-up steps, a sales pipeline, a hiring process. For flows that split and join use sankey-chart; for amounts that are not a sequence use bar-chart horizontal.

```tsx
<FunnelChart
  label="Sign-up steps"
  data={[
    { step: "Visited", people: 1200 },
    { step: "Started", people: 640 },
    { step: "Confirmed email", people: 410 },
    { step: "Finished", people: 290 },
  ]}
  x="step"
  value="people"
/>
```

### gantt-chart

Tasks as bars along a time axis, one row each, under optional group headings: how far each has got, which must finish before another starts (arrows), milestones as diamonds and a line for today, with Up and Down reading each task.

Use it: Planning or reporting work over time: a project plan, a release schedule, a timeline of events with lengths. For events without length use timeline (a list) or a line-chart annotation; for a calendar of single days use calendar or calendar-heatmap.

```tsx
<GanttChart
  label="Launch plan"
  tasks={[
    { id: "design", label: "Design", start: "2026-03-02", end: "2026-03-13", group: "Product", progress: 1 },
    { id: "build", label: "Build", start: "2026-03-09", end: "2026-04-03", group: "Product", progress: 0.4, dependsOn: ["design"] },
    { id: "launch", label: "Launch", start: "2026-04-06", end: "2026-04-06", group: "Marketing", milestone: true, dependsOn: ["build"] },
  ]}
  today="2026-03-20"
/>
```

### geo-hexbin

A geo-map layer that gathers many points into hexagons or squares of equal size on screen, each coloured on one hue by how many points (or how much weight) fall in it, re-gathered as the map zooms; each cell read by arrow keys and listed in a table.

Use it: Thousands of points where single marks would pile up: sightings, incidents, trips, addresses. For a few dozen named places use geo-markers; for values that belong to regions use choropleth. Goes inside geo-map.

```tsx
<GeoMap label="Sightings" fit={area}>
  <GeoFeatures data={area} />
  <GeoHexbin label="Sightings" points={sightings} radius={14} valueLabel="Sightings" />
</GeoMap>
```

### geo-map

A map drawn from GeoJSON the project passes (no tiles, no hosted data), in any d3-geo projection fitted to its box, zoomed and panned by dragging, pinching, Ctrl and the wheel, a double click, buttons or keys, with parts for a graticule, plain shapes, a scale bar, and layers that are read item by item by arrow keys.

Use it: Showing places, regions or routes from data the project holds: a choropleth, sites on a map, flows between cities. Add layers inside it: choropleth, geo-markers, geo-routes, geo-hexbin, geo-tiles. Inside layout/map-frame it loads only when asked. For a street map with search and directions, bring a map engine and put it in map-frame; for a spinning globe as decoration use three/globe.

```tsx
<GeoMap label="Regions of the study area" fit={regions} projection="equal-earth">
  <GeoGraticule />
  <GeoFeatures data={regions} />
  <GeoMarkers label="Sites" points={[{ id: "a", name: "Site A", lon: 10.7, lat: 59.9 }]} />
  <GeoScaleBar />
</GeoMap>
```

### geo-markers

A geo-map layer of places: points in their group's colour and shape with optional names, or bubbles whose area is a number; each read by arrow keys and listed in a table.

Use it: Marking sites, cities or events on a map, or comparing counts by place (bubbles: area, never radius, carries the number). For values that belong to whole regions use choropleth; for thousands of points use geo-hexbin. Goes inside geo-map.

```tsx
<GeoMap label="Our stores" fit={country}>
  <GeoFeatures data={country} />
  <GeoMarkers
    label="Stores"
    points={[
      { id: "a", name: "Harbour", lon: 5.32, lat: 60.39, value: 120 },
      { id: "b", name: "Station", lon: 10.75, lat: 59.91, value: 340 },
    ]}
    variant="bubble"
    valueLabel="Visits"
  />
</GeoMap>
```

### geo-routes

A geo-map layer of journeys and flows between places: great-circle routes (the shortest way over the globe) or arcs drawn over the map, thicker for larger amounts, with an arrow for the direction; each read by arrow keys and listed in a table.

Use it: Showing movement between places: flights, deliveries, migration, trade. Keep to a few dozen routes, or aggregate them first. For flows without geography use sankey-chart or chord-diagram. Goes inside geo-map.

```tsx
<GeoMap label="Flights from the hub" projection="natural-earth">
  <GeoGraticule />
  <GeoRoutes
    label="Flights"
    routes={[
      { id: "1", name: "Hub to Port", from: [10.7, 59.9], to: [-74, 40.7], value: 12 },
      { id: "2", name: "Hub to Cape", from: [10.7, 59.9], to: [18.4, -33.9], value: 4 },
    ]}
    valueLabel="Flights a week"
  />
</GeoMap>
```

### geo-tiles

A geo-map layer of raster map tiles from an address template the project gives ("…/{z}/{x}/{y}.png"), placed under the other layers and following the zoom, with the attribution the tile provider asks for. It has no default address: nothing is fetched unless the project names a server.

Use it: A geo-map needs a picture of streets or terrain under the data and the project has a tile server it may use (its own, or a provider whose terms it accepts). Use projection="mercator" (tiles are drawn in Web Mercator). Tiles come from a third party, so put the map in layout/map-frame with a MapFrameNotice and nothing is requested before the person asks. Without tiles, draw shapes with GeoFeatures.

```tsx
<GeoMap label="Delivery area" fit={area} projection="mercator">
  <GeoTiles url="https://tiles.example.org/{z}/{x}/{y}.png" attribution="© Example contributors" />
  <GeoFeatures data={area} variant="line" />
</GeoMap>
```

### heatmap

A matrix of cells (day by hour, for example) coloured on one-hue scale from faint to the highlight colour, with a tooltip, arrow-key reading and a scale legend.

Use it: Spotting patterns across two categories at once: when it is busy, which pairs stand out. To compare exact amounts use bar-chart; for one row of values over time use line-chart.

```tsx
<Heatmap
  label="Sessions by day and hour"
  data={[
    { day: "Mon", hour: "09", sessions: 12 },
    { day: "Mon", hour: "10", sessions: 30 },
    { day: "Tue", hour: "09", sessions: 8 },
    { day: "Tue", hour: "10", sessions: 21 },
  ]}
  x="hour"
  y="day"
  value="sessions"
/>
```

### histogram

How the values of one measure are spread: the range cut into equal bins, each bar as tall as the number of values that fall in it, with arrow-key reading of each bin.

Use it: Seeing the shape of a distribution: where most values are, how wide, whether there are two humps or a long tail. To compare the spread of several groups use box-plot; to compare totals across categories use bar-chart.

```tsx
<Histogram
  label="Delivery times"
  data={[{ minutes: 22 }, { minutes: 31 }, { minutes: 28 }, { minutes: 45 }, { minutes: 26 }, { minutes: 33 }]}
  value="minutes"
  valueLabel="Minutes"
  bins={8}
/>
```

### line-chart

A line chart of one or more series over a numeric or time x, with a crosshair tooltip, arrow-key reading and labels at the line ends.

Use it: Change over time or along a number, for up to about five series on one shared scale. For a single series whose volume matters use area-chart; for separate categories use bar-chart; never plot two different units against two y axes, use two charts.

```tsx
<LineChart
  label="Requests and errors per day"
  data={[
    { day: new Date("2026-03-01"), requests: 120, errors: 4 },
    { day: new Date("2026-03-02"), requests: 180, errors: 9 },
    { day: new Date("2026-03-03"), requests: 150, errors: 3 },
  ]}
  x="day"
  series={[
    { key: "requests", label: "Requests" },
    { key: "errors", label: "Errors" },
  ]}
/>
```

### network-graph

Things and the links between them, placed by a force layout that is run to rest before it is drawn (so it is the same every time and never moves on its own), with each node's links lit on hover or focus and every node reachable by arrow keys.

Use it: Showing who or what is connected to what: clusters, bridges between groups, the most linked items. Keep it to a few hundred nodes. For amounts flowing in one direction use sankey-chart; for a hierarchy use treemap or tree-view; for a process the person edits use flow-diagram.

```tsx
<NetworkGraph
  label="Libraries and what they use"
  nodes={[{ id: "app", group: "Apps" }, { id: "ui", group: "Libraries" }, { id: "charts", group: "Libraries" }, { id: "maths", group: "Libraries" }]}
  links={[{ source: "app", target: "ui" }, { source: "app", target: "charts" }, { source: "charts", target: "maths" }]}
/>
```

### parallel-coordinates

Many measures of many things at once: one upright axis per measure, each thing a line that crosses every axis at its value, so trade-offs and clusters show as patterns of crossing or parallel lines; each line lit and read by arrow keys.

Use it: Comparing things across four to ten measures with different units: cars by price, power and weight; plans by cost and limits. For two measures use scatter-chart; for a few things on one scale use radar-chart; for exact values use table or data-grid.

```tsx
<ParallelCoordinates
  label="Laptops compared"
  data={[
    { name: "Alder", price: 900, weight: 1.3, battery: 12, kind: "Light" },
    { name: "Birch", price: 1400, weight: 2.1, battery: 8, kind: "Power" },
    { name: "Cedar", price: 700, weight: 1.6, battery: 10, kind: "Light" },
  ]}
  dimensions={[{ key: "price", label: "Price" }, { key: "weight", label: "Weight (kg)" }, { key: "battery", label: "Battery (h)" }]}
  name="name"
  group="kind"
/>
```

### radar-chart

Several measures on spokes around a centre, one closed shape per series, so profiles can be compared at a glance: which is stronger where, with arrow keys reading each spoke.

Use it: Comparing two or three profiles across five to ten measures on the same scale: skills, product ratings, nutrition against a target. For exact comparison, or measures on different scales, use bar-chart or small-multiples; with more than three series the shapes tangle.

```tsx
<RadarChart
  label="Two plans compared"
  data={[
    { measure: "Speed", basic: 3, plus: 4 },
    { measure: "Storage", basic: 2, plus: 5 },
    { measure: "Support", basic: 3, plus: 4 },
    { measure: "Price", basic: 5, plus: 3 },
    { measure: "Security", basic: 4, plus: 4 },
  ]}
  axis="measure"
  series={[{ key: "basic", label: "Basic" }, { key: "plus", label: "Plus" }]}
  max={5}
/>
```

### radial-progress

A ring gauge for one value against a limit, with the value and a label in the centre.

Use it: One ratio: a quota used, a score, a goal reached. Size it with a width class (`w-32` by default). For several ratios side by side use a list of bars (bar-chart horizontal), not a ring each; for parts of a whole use donut-chart.

```tsx
<RadialProgress value={72} label="Storage used" />
<RadialProgress value={3} max={5} label="Steps done" formatValue={(value) => `${value} of 5`} className="w-40" />
```

### sankey-chart

Flows between stages as bands whose widths are the amounts: where a total comes from, where it goes and what is lost on the way, with every node and band reachable by arrow keys.

Use it: Showing how amounts move through steps or between categories: a budget from sources to uses, visitors through a sign-up, energy from fuel to use. For a single funnel of shrinking steps use funnel-chart; for links without amounts use network-graph; for two-way flows between the same groups use chord-diagram.

```tsx
<SankeyChart
  label="Where the money goes"
  nodes={[{ id: "income", label: "Income" }, { id: "rent", label: "Rent" }, { id: "food", label: "Food" }, { id: "saved", label: "Saved" }]}
  links={[
    { source: "income", target: "rent", value: 1200 },
    { source: "income", target: "food", value: 500 },
    { source: "income", target: "saved", value: 300 },
  ]}
/>
```

### scatter-chart

Points placed by two numbers, optionally sized by a third (a bubble chart) and grouped by a category, with the nearest point read under the pointer and every point reachable by arrow keys.

Use it: Showing how two measures relate across many things: does one rise with the other, which stand apart. Give `size` for a third measure as bubble area. For change over time use line-chart; for one measure across categories use bar-chart or dot-plot; for thousands of overlapping points use density-chart.

```tsx
<ScatterChart
  label="Price against rating"
  data={[
    { name: "Alder", price: 12, rating: 4.1, sold: 320, kind: "Tea" },
    { name: "Birch", price: 18, rating: 4.6, sold: 120, kind: "Tea" },
    { name: "Cedar", price: 9, rating: 3.8, sold: 540, kind: "Coffee" },
  ]}
  x="price"
  y="rating"
  size="sold"
  group="kind"
  name="name"
  xLabel="Price"
  yLabel="Rating"
/>
```

### slope-chart

Each thing's value at two moments joined by a line, so what rose, what fell and how the ranking changed read at once: names and values at both ends, rises solid and falls dashed so direction never rests on colour.

Use it: Comparing many things between exactly two moments or conditions: this year and last, before and after a change. For many moments use line-chart or small-multiples; for one thing's change use a stat with its delta; for a few categories use dot-plot dumbbell.

```tsx
<SlopeChart
  label="Share of trips by mode"
  data={[
    { mode: "Car", y2016: 52, y2026: 41 },
    { mode: "Bike", y2016: 9, y2026: 18 },
    { mode: "Transit", y2016: 24, y2026: 27 },
  ]}
  name="mode"
  from="y2016"
  to="y2026"
  fromLabel="2016"
  toLabel="2026"
/>
```

### small-multiples

The same small chart repeated for each group (a region, a product) in a grid that fits its width, every panel on one shared scale so they can be compared at a glance, each read by arrow keys.

Use it: Comparing the shape of one measure across many groups, where one chart with many lines would tangle: more than five series, or groups of very different sizes. For up to five series on one chart use line-chart; for one value per group use bar-chart.

```tsx
<SmallMultiples
  label="Monthly visits by region"
  data={[
    { region: "North", month: 1, visits: 40 }, { region: "North", month: 2, visits: 52 }, { region: "North", month: 3, visits: 61 },
    { region: "South", month: 1, visits: 30 }, { region: "South", month: 2, visits: 28 }, { region: "South", month: 3, visits: 35 },
  ]}
  facet="region"
  x="month"
  y="visits"
  kind="area"
/>
```

### sparkline

A tiny line, area or bar chart with no axes, for a stat tile or a table cell, described in words for assistive technology.

Use it: The shape of a trend beside a number that carries the value. Size it with classes (`h-8 w-24` by default). When the reader needs to read values off it, use line-chart or bar-chart.

```tsx
<Sparkline data={[4, 6, 5, 9, 12, 10, 14]} label="Signups, last 7 days" />
<Sparkline data={[3, 8, 2, 7, 5]} type="bar" className="h-6 w-16" />
```

### stream-chart

Several series stacked as flowing layers around a centre line instead of a baseline (a streamgraph), so the rise and fall of each layer and of the whole read as a shape over time; arrow keys read every moment.

Use it: Showing how the mix of up to five categories shifts over a long time, where the overall shape matters more than exact values: listening by genre, topics over years. For exact totals use area-chart stacked (with a baseline); for exact values per series use line-chart.

```tsx
<StreamChart
  label="Plays by genre"
  data={[
    { year: 2020, jazz: 20, folk: 30, rock: 50 },
    { year: 2021, jazz: 28, folk: 34, rock: 44 },
    { year: 2022, jazz: 40, folk: 30, rock: 38 },
  ]}
  x="year"
  series={[{ key: "jazz", label: "Jazz" }, { key: "folk", label: "Folk" }, { key: "rock", label: "Rock" }]}
/>
```

### sunburst

A hierarchy as rings around a centre: each ring a level, each arc a part sized by its share of its parent, with zooming into any arc by click or Enter and back out by the centre, the trail or Backspace.

Use it: Showing how a total divides level by level when the depth matters as much as the sizes: a path through categories, a file system, a budget in three levels. For sizes that must be compared closely use treemap (areas in rectangles are easier to judge than arcs); for one level use donut-chart.

```tsx
<Sunburst
  label="Visits by source"
  data={{
    name: "All visits",
    children: [
      { name: "Search", children: [{ name: "Organic", value: 420 }, { name: "Paid", value: 160 }] },
      { name: "Social", children: [{ name: "Video", value: 120 }, { name: "Posts", value: 80 }] },
      { name: "Direct", value: 300 },
    ],
  }}
/>
```

### treemap

A whole split into nested rectangles whose areas are the parts' sizes: groups in their own colours, the parts inside them labelled where they fit, with zooming into a group by click or Enter and back out by the trail or Backspace.

Use it: Showing how a large total divides across a hierarchy (a budget by department and team, storage by folder) when there are too many parts for a donut. For a few parts use donut-chart; to see the levels as rings use sunburst; to compare exact sizes use bar-chart.

```tsx
<Treemap
  label="Spending by area"
  data={{
    name: "All spending",
    children: [
      { name: "Housing", children: [{ name: "Rent", value: 1200 }, { name: "Power", value: 140 }] },
      { name: "Food", children: [{ name: "Groceries", value: 420 }, { name: "Cafés", value: 90 }] },
      { name: "Travel", value: 260 },
    ],
  }}
/>
```

### waterfall-chart

How a starting amount becomes an ending one, step by step: each rise or fall a bar floating from the running total, totals standing on the baseline, signs printed on every step so rises and falls never rest on colour.

Use it: Explaining a change between two totals: a budget's start to its end, revenue to profit, last year to this year by cause. For parts of one total use bar-chart stacked or treemap; for change over time use line-chart.

```tsx
<WaterfallChart
  label="From revenue to profit"
  data={[
    { step: "Revenue", amount: 500, total: true },
    { step: "Costs", amount: -220 },
    { step: "Marketing", amount: -80 },
    { step: "Other income", amount: 30 },
    { step: "Profit", amount: 230, total: true },
  ]}
  x="step"
  value="amount"
  total="total"
/>
```
